Seeing that best of beings then about to take the soma for the Aśvins, / the god Indra, slayer of Bala, said this word: / 14
"If you yourself will take the soma for the sake of these two, / I will strike you with the thunderbolt, terrible and unsurpassed." / 15
Being thus addressed, that descendant of Bhṛgu, looking directly at Indra, / took the excellent soma libation-cup for the two Aśvins according to rule. / 16
Then in anger Indra, lord of Śacī, hurled his thunderbolt at him; / as he was hurling it, the descendant of Bhṛgu paralysed his arm. / 17
Having paralysed it, Cyavana of great splendour then offered into the fire with mantras, / seeking to create an evil spirit, intent on destroying the god. / 18

paralysed in form with fear, repeatedly licking his lips, / bowed down, O great goddess, and afflicted with terror, said to Cyavana:
'From this day forward, O descendant of Bhṛgu, these two Aśvins shall be worthy of soma; / all this will come to pass; I tell you true words.
[167b]
Let your undertaking not be in vain, O rich in austerity; / and I know, O brahmin-seer, that you will not act in vain.
Just as these two Aśvins have today been made worthy of soma by you, / so indeed may your prowess be revealed yet further, O descendant of Bhṛgu,
and may there be fame in the world for the father of Sukanyā. / Therefore, this revelation of your prowess was brought about by me.
Therefore, show me grace; let this be as you desire.'
When addressed thus by Śakra, the wrath of high-souled Cyavana / quickly subsided, as did the pride of the lord of the gods.
And the mighty [Cyavana], O goddess, divided Mada, who was previously created, again and again / into drink, women, dice, and hunting.

8.9.m:
Having thus distributed Mada and satisfied Śakra with soma,
and having caused that king to sacrifice together with all accompanied by the two Aśvins, / having proclaimed his power in all worlds, O lady of fair complexion,
he sported with Sukanyā in this sacred field in the great forest. / Linked with him, O goddess, bearing the name Cyavaneśvara,
is the liṅga installed by Cyavana, which removes great sins. / Whoever worships it according to rule obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha.
Therefore seers wait upon Candramasastīrtha, / seers named Vaikhānasa and likewise Vālakhilyas.
A man who performs a śrāddha here according to rule, particularly on the full moon in the month of Āśvina, / and feeds brahmins separately,
shall obtain the fruit of ten million tīrthas; of this there is no doubt.
A person who listens to this story which destroys sins, O goddess, / will be liberated from sin generated in all births.

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the excellent pool of Sukanyā, / where the two Aśvins submerged themselves along with Cyavana, O Ambikā,
where Cyavana became equal in form to the Aśvins.
Where Sukanyā of fair complexion obtained her desire / through the power of bathing in the pool; hence it is called Kanyāsaras.
An auspicious woman who bathes there, especially on the third lunar day,
shall not suffer the ruin of her household for seven thousand births, / nor will her husband become poor, deformed, miserable, or blind.

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go again to the Nyaṅkumatī river; / having performed the Gayā-śrāddha there at the excellent Goṣpada tīrtha,
one should then view Varāha, and from there go to the abode of Hari. / Having worshipped the Mothers there and bathed at the confluence with the ocean,
where the Nyaṅkumatī meets the sea, one should then proceed towards the east / to the divine hermitage of Agastya, known as that which removes hunger,
where the venerable sage, having slain Ilvala and Vātāpi, / and having freed the brahmins from dangers, then gave them that place.
[168a]
This is indeed the hermitage of Agastya, beloved of Agasti and most excellent, / on the delightful bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, destroying all sins.

8.9.m:
Why was Vātāpi destroyed here by Agastya? / What was the power of that Daitya who was the destroyer of brahmins here?
And for what reason did the anger of high-souled Agasti arise?
Īśvara said:
Formerly, in the city of Maṇimatī, O lady of fair complexion, there was a lord of Daityas named Ilvala, / and Vātāpi was his younger brother.
That son of Diti said to a brahmin endowed with austerity: / 'O venerable one, grant me a son equal to Indra.'
When that brahmin did not wish to give such a son to him, / the son of Diti became intensely angry with that brahmin.
Having arrived at Prabhāsa-kṣetra, that evil-minded Daitya— / and Vātāpi took the form of a ram, capable of assuming any form at will in an instant—
wishing to kill brahmins there, he would cook [him] and feed them; / and then he would summon by speech the one who had met destruction.
Assuming his body again, he would appear alive. / Then Vātāpi, having turned himself into a well-cooked goat,

Tearing open the side of that great-souled brahmin, / laughing aloud, Vātāpi came forth there from the twice-born's belly.
Thus feeding the brahmins again and again, O goddess, / and bursting open their bellies, he would slay many twice-borns.
Then indeed, terrified with fear, all the brahmins fled. / They went to the hermitage of Agastya and spoke before [him]:
“O lord, hear our words, bringing terror to us! / We have all been invited, O master, by Ilvala.
That meal is the form of death for us; there is no doubt. / Therefore protect us, O lord, whose minds are dejected and despairing!”
Then having arrived at Prabhāsa, where those two foremost daityas were, / killers of brahmins and delighting in sin, that great sage beheld them.
Having seen that great asura Vātāpi prepared in the form of a ram, / he said: “Give me food; hunger has come upon me.”

8.9.m:
Being thus spoken to, the two then bid welcome to the sage there: / “O lord, I shall give you food in great abundance.
Of what measure is your food? So much measure shall I cook.”
Agastya said:
“Cook the food, O king of daityas; there will be some satisfaction.” / Saying “So be it,” the king of daityas said it was cooked, O great sage.
“Let this seat be taken; eat according to your wish, O sage!” / Being thus spoken to, muttering the Aghora mantra that brings about the end of an aeon,
and then taking a prominent seat, the great sage sat down.
Ilvala, the king of daityas, served him as if laughing. / He made a heap of food a hundred cubits in measure.
Then, delighted in mind, Agastya swallowed two mouthfuls, / having assumed a vast form just as in the drying up of the ocean.
Then he consumed the whole of that food, [namely] Vātāpi. / When he had eaten, the asura Ilvala called out to him.

Then he who had given the food to the great-souled Agastya— / he reduced to ashes all that food together with the dānava.
With a fist of wrath, the great sage reduced Ilvala to ashes. / Then, raising a cry of lamentation, all the daityas perished.
[Folio] 168b
Then Agastya of great splendor summoned the foremost of the twice-born / and gave them that place, filled with the wealth of the daityas.
Because the hunger of Agastya was removed there by the dānavas, O goddess, / therefore there arose the place of the twice-born named Kṣudhāhara.
On the western side of it, situated not very far away, / is that known as Gaṅgeśvara, which was established by Gaṅgā. / Formerly, at the eating of Vātāpi, by the great-souled Agastya, / for the purification of all sin born of consuming the daitya,
Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sin, was summoned, O great goddess.
Then, O goddess, Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sin, arrived. / She effected the purification of that ṛṣi and remained standing in that place,

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to Bālārka, which destroys sins, / not very far to the north from the hermitage of Agastya, O goddess,
where the sun, while still a boy, formerly performed austerity, O dear one; / therefore this name “Bālārka” became famous on the earth.
Beholding him on a Sunday, a man does not become afflicted with leprosy; / the suffering born of disease among children shall never occur.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled “Description of the Māhātmya of Bālārka,” in the first [part], the Māhātmya of the Prabhāsakṣetra, in the seventh [book], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses].
Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to auspicious Ajāpāleśvarī, / situated not very far to the east of the site of Agastya.
Ajāpāla, the best of kings, was born in the lineage of Raghu; / he, having worshipped the goddess there, who subjugates sins and diseases,
the king indeed grazed the diseases that had assumed the form of goats. / There he installed that destroyer of sin under his own name.
A man who worships her with devotion according to the rite on the third lunar day / shall attain strength, intellect, fame, learning, and good fortune.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled “Description of the Māhātmya of Ajāpāleśvarī,” in the first [part], the Māhātmya of the Prabhāsakṣetra, in the seventh [book], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses].

8.9.m:
Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to that known as Bālāditya, / two gavyūtis to the east of the site of Agastya.
To the south of that place named Sapāṭikā is situated, / at a distance of a single gavyūti, O ruler of the gods, the one well known as Bālārka,
where learning was worshipped by the wise Viśvāmitra; / having set up a triad of liṅgas and having likewise installed the sun,
he performed the accomplishment of the lore and attained perfection from the sun. / Therefore that lord attained renown as “Bālāditya” from that time on.
[Folio] 169a
Beholding him, O goddess, the sun that steals away sins, / a man does not suffer poverty as long as he lives.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled “Description of the Māhātmya of Bālārka,” in the first [part], the Māhātmya of the Prabhāsakṣetra, in the seventh [book], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses].

To the south of that very place, O goddess, just a gavyūti away from it, / the Gaṅgā flowing to Pātāla is situated, destroying sins.
And it was invoked by Viśvāmitra for bathing, O lady of fair complexion! / Having bathed there, O great goddess, one is freed from all sins. // 2
Seeing Gaṅgeśvara there, and likewise Viśvāmitreśvara, / and beholding Bāleśvara, one obtains all desires. // 3

8.9.m:
How did he, having been a brahmin, become a thief, the lowest of men? / Tell me that, O Lord of the gods, how he became Dhanada. // 3
Īśvara said:
Regarding that matter, O great goddess, what happened in the reign of Uttama [Manu], / I will narrate all that, indicating the greatness of Śiva. // 4
There was a certain twice-born, O goddess, renowned by the name Devaśarman; / residing in the Prabhāsakṣetra, he dwelt on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī. // 5
Ever devoted solely to business concerning his sons, fields, wife, and the like, / he then abandoned householdership, deluded by greed for wealth;
he wandered through this earth along with its villages and towns. // 6
His wife, having tremulous eyes, went out from his house; / always wandering at her own will, she was continually infatuated by love. // 7
From her, by the power of destiny, a son was once born from a śūdra; / extremely wicked-minded, unrestrained, he was therefore named Duḥsaha. // 8
Then, with the passage of much time, he engaged in deeds fitting his name; / stricken by vices, sinful, he was abandoned likewise by his kinsfolk. // 9

8.9.m:
Seeing in a certain temple of Śiva wealth serving as articles of worship, / at the beginning of the thick of night, desiring to steal it, he entered then. // 10
As the lamp was almost extinguished, its wick about to be cut, / a wick was offered by him for the sake of searching for the wealth. // 11
Awakened, the man performing the worship of the deity rose there; / holding an iron bar as a weapon, he cried out loudly: "Who is this? Who is this?" // 12
And he, born of a śūdra, fled out of fear for his life, dull-witted, / reviling his own birth and deeds, exceedingly sorrowful. // 13
Struck down on the earth by the city guards, he died from the passage of time. / He became a king in the region of Gandhāra, celebrated by the name Sudurmukha. // 14
There, fond of singing and instrumental music, he was exceedingly attached to courtesans; / causing distress to his subjects, foolish, he was excluded from all dharma. // 15

To the north of that place called Kaurava, / the great goddess Bhadrakālī, having performed severe austerity, (1)
installed the Sun, endowed with supreme devotion, / on a Sunday on the seventh lunar day, with red flowers and unguents. (2)
Whoever worships him with devotion obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices, / and is freed from ailments arising from wind and bile, and many others. (3)
A horse should be given right there by those desiring the full fruit of the pilgrimage. (4)

The Lord said:
To the south-west of that place of Vaiśravaṇa, O fair-complexioned one, / resides Kubera himself, the destroyer of all poverty, (1)
adorned with the eight treasures beginning with Makara. / One should worship him with devotion on the fifth lunar day with fragrant perfumes, flowers, and unguents;

8.9.m:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the east of the Kaubera [shrine], / five gavyūtis away, O goddess, to the place named Puṣkara by name,
where a Kaivarta, a killer of fish, achieved perfection, O great goddess. (1)
The goddess said:
Tell me in detail how he indeed attained perfection. / Relate it through your grace, O god of gods, O Maheśvara. (2)
170b
The Lord said:
Listen, O goddess, to what happened formerly in the Svārociṣa Manvantara. / There was a certain ill-behaved Kaivarta, a killer of fish. (3)
Wandering about at one time, that sinner went to Puṣkara. / He saw a temple belonging to Śaṅkara, overgrown with creepers and trees. (4)
Tormented by the cold in the month of Māgha, and carrying a wet net, / the afflicted man climbed onto the temple seeking to catch the heat of the sun. (5)
Then, to dry that wet net by the rays of the sun, / he spread it out on the tip of the flagpole of the temple. (6)
Then, O goddess, due to numbness from the cold, he fell from the temple; / he died suddenly, O goddess, in that sacred field of Śiva. (7)

8.9.m:
Since that net of his, through the lapse of much time, / was tied as a banner by means of the nets, it became auspicious upon the temple. (8)
Then, by the majesty of the banner, he was born on earth as a ruler of men, / the wise one renowned as Ṛtadhvaja in the Saurāṣṭra country.
He traversed the earth on a chariot with a shining banner at the front. (9)
Overpowered by sensory pleasures, the mighty king ruled. / Then, in the temple of Śambhu, the lord offered a beautiful, (10)
bright, and multi-coloured banner, and nothing else at all.
Then the king, remembering his past lives, came to the Prabhāsa-kṣetra. / There, to that shrine filled with an array of banners, (11)
and of the god Ajogandha, who was worshipped previously, / he caused a temple to be built, as well as the utensils for Śiva's worship. (12)
With devotion he perpetually worshipped that liṅga which destroys sin. / The high-minded one ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years. (13)
By the power of that liṅga, he went to heaven when his time came. / Therefore, having gone there with diligent effort, one should worship the liṅga, (14)

Situated not very far to the north of that, / O goddess, is where Candrodaka is, which destroys old age and poverty. // 2
Its increase happens with the waxing of the moon, and its decrease with its waning; / even in this age of sin, it is occasionally seen thus. // 3
Having bathed there, O great goddess, even if a thousand sins / have been committed, he attains [purification] here; no doubt should be entertained on this matter. // 4
There, by Indra, who was terrified of the great sin arising from his encounter with Ahalyā, / whose mind had been confounded by the curse originating from Gautama, // 5

and who performed sacrifices with lavish priestly gifts long ago, O goddess, / having established Śiva, the Lord, there for thousands of years,
under the name Indreśvara, which indeed destroys all sins. // 6

Īśvara said:
To the southeast of that, at a distance of seven gavyūtis, / is the place named Devakula, where the gods gather. // 1
Where the seers and siddhas were long ago when the liṅga fell, / and because it arose [there], O great goddess, it is remembered as Devakula. // 2
To the west of it is the great river Ṛṣitoyā, / dear to the seers, O goddess, and destroying all sins. // 3
Having bathed there properly, if a man offers water to the ancestors, / he brings satisfaction to the ancestors for indeed seventy thousand years. // 4
Gold should be given there, as well as an antelope skin and a blanket; / whatever is given on the new moon of Āṣāḍha, surely, // 5
increases sixteenfold until the full moon arrives. // 6

The goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, savior across the ocean of worldly existence, / tell me in detail about the great emergence of Ṛṣitoyā. // 1
How did that name, 'Ṛṣitoyā', become known upon the surface of the earth? / And how did she come again to the auspicious Devadāru forest? // 2
Īśvara said:
Listen, O goddess, attentively to my words, and I shall tell / the glory of the Ṛṣitoyā, which destroys all sins. // 3
In the holy Devadāru forest, seers endowed with austerity, / by the hundreds and thousands, dwelled, O woman of shapely hips. // 4

As they lived there, a long time passed, O beloved; / having multiplied with sons and grandsons, they remained occupying the Dāruka [forest]. // 5
They all assembled and reflected among themselves: / 'The highly sacred Sarasvatī, bearing the submarine fire on her head, // 6

Īśvara said:

and praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, with various hymns of praise. // 9
The seers said:

Seeing all [of them] that were to go toward the earth, / the Grandfather [looked] toward the delightful Devadāru forest in the excellent sacred field of Prabhāsa.
He cast his gaze upon his water pot, and they entered the water pot. / Brahmā said:
"All the extremely holy rivers have been gathered into Brahmā's water pot. / Having entered [it], let them go to the earth out of compassion for the seers.
If I dispatch only one, O twice-born, the others will surely be angry with me. / Therefore, I shall release all of them that have merged into the water pot."
Īśvara said:
Then Brahmā released the great rivers that were present there. / Having released them, Brahmā addressed all the sages repeatedly:

Īśvara said:
Thus, O goddess, the river arrived in the Devadāru forest, / renowned as Ṛṣitoyā, pure, O fair-faced one.
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and auspicious Vedic chants, / the goddess was brought to the ocean by the seers versed in the Vedas.
Everywhere the goddess is easily accessible, but in three places she is hard to attain: / at the Mahodaya, in the great tīrtha, in the presence of Mūlacaṇḍīśa,
and where she flows eastward, joining the sea. / Where Ṛṣitoyā is found, what more is sought there?
Those men who drink her water are forever blessed; / [in it] bones dissolve within six months.
In the morning the Gaṅgā flows, and in the evening the Yamunā.
At midday the Sarasvatī joined by a thousand rivers; / in the afternoon the Revā flows, and at twilight the daughter of Sūrya.

This Prayāga, the king of tīrthas, arrived; / surrounded by crores of tīrthas, he concealed himself.

all the foremost gods, led by Brahmā, stood there, O goddess.

Having spoken thus, the Great God remained in that place, O beloved. / Three pools are recorded there: of Brahmā, of Viṣṇu, and of Rudra.
The fourth is called Trisaṅgama, where there is the confluence of the rivers: / of the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and the daughter of Sūrya.
One crore of tīrthas resides in the pool of Brahmā; / likewise, one crore is proclaimed in the pool of Viṣṇu.
A crore and a half is proclaimed in the pool of Śiva. / The pool of Brahmā is in the west, and that of Viṣṇu in the east;
and the one in the middle is known as the pool of Rudra. / Emerging from the middle of the pool, where the Gaṅgā, O fair-faced one,
meets with the daughter of Sūrya, that is called Trisaṅgama. / Between these two, subtly hidden, is the Sarasvatī.
Prayāga, the lord of tīrthas, is perpetually present in these. / A man who comes here in the month of Māgha, O fair-faced one,

A bull should be given there by those who wish for the full fruit of the pilgrimage; / for one who undertakes the pilgrimage thus, the fruit is endless.
In this way the māhātmya of Guptaprayāga has been related to you. / Hearing it and receiving it with joy, a man attains the abode of Śaṃkara.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, entitled ‘Description of the Māhātmya of Guptaprayāga’, in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh [book], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the venerable Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

8.9.m:
On its southern side, situated not very far away, / resides Mādhava, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, fasting and with senses subdued, / he who worships him with devotion using fragrant perfumes, flowers, and unguents,
goes to the supreme abode that grants freedom from rebirth.
Here a verse was formerly sung by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds: / ‘The man who bathes in Viṣṇukuṇḍa and worships Mādhava,
shall go to the supreme abode / where the god Hari himself dwells.’
All this māhātmya dedicated to Viṣṇu has been related to you, / granting all desires to men and destroying all mortal sins.

8.9.m:
To the northern side of that very place, situated somewhat to the north-west, / is [the liṅga] named Saṃgāleśvara, which destroys all mortal sins.
There Brahmā and Viṣṇu set about worshipping the liṅga; / and Śakra, of great splendor, worshipped the liṅga, O beloved.
Varuṇa, Dhanada, Dharmarāja, and Pāvaka, / together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Lokapālas on all sides,
worshipped the great liṅga bearing the name Saṃgāleśvara. / Having worshipped it, they all beheld its supreme māhātmya,
and, filled with supreme bliss, they suddenly said, O goddess: / ‘Because it was established by the hosts of gods coming together,
its name upon earth shall be Saṃgāleśvara.
Men shall worship the one named Saṃgāleśvara; / no one in their family shall ever be destitute of wealth.
Whatever fruit is obtained from donating a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra, / that same fruit one obtains from the darśana of Saṃgāleśvara.’

8.9.m:
And on the new moon day, having performed ritual ablution according to rule, / whatever man performs a śrāddha for the ancestors, free from anger,
his ancestors are satisfied until the destruction of all elements.
That sacred field extends for half a krośa all around in circumference; / it grants all desires to men and destroys all mortal sins.
In this sacred field, O great goddess, living beings, high or middling, / who meet their end through the course of time, also go to the supreme state.
Those men who take a vow of fasting and cast off their breaths of life, / surely, O great goddess, merge into the Supreme Lord.
Those killed by cows, those killed by twice-born, and those killed by tusked beasts, / those who take their own lives, and those who die of snakebite,
those who lose their breath of life in bed, and those devoid of purity— / in this greatly holy sacred ford that grants freedom from rebirth,
when the sixteen śrāddhas are given, a bull is set free, / and brahmins are fed according to rule, their liberation is beyond doubt.

Having spoken thus, all the gods went to heaven.
The māhātmya of Saṃgāleśvara has been told to you in brief; / when heard, it removes sins as well as pain and grief.
Thus ends the three hundredth chapter, entitled ‘Description of the Māhātmya of Saṃgāleśvara’, in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh [book], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the venerable Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to unexcelled Siddheśvara, / situated on the eastern side of that very place, not far away.
When the gods assembled and swiftly consecrated the Śiva-liṅga / endowed with the name Saṃgāleśvara, auspicious and taking away all sins,
then all the hosts of siddhas worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord / and established a liṅga that grants all accomplishments,
endowed with the name Siddheśvara, destroying great sins. / Then the hosts of siddhas praised Śiva with various hymns.

8.9.m:
Thereupon Mahādeva, well-pleased, said: ‘Ask for an excellent boon.’ / Then they all bowed to the Moon-crested Lord and said:
‘Whichever man comes here, bathes according to rule, / worships Siddhanātha, and recites the Śatarudrīya,
or recites the Aghora mantra, or the Gāyatrī dedicated to Maheśvara, / if he recites it within six months, O best of sages,
he will surely attain the siddhi of sovereignty with the qualities such as lightness and the rest.’
Īśvara said:
Saying ‘So shall it be,’ Hara vanished. / Having worshipped Siddheśvara, a man should recite the Aghora [mantra]
at midnight on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina; / taking courage, fearless, that man shall attain perfection.
Thus has this sin-destroying māhātmya of the god Siddheśvara, / granting the fruits of all desires, been related, O goddess.

Whoever worships that god who was formerly worshipped by serpents— / poison does not affect his body as long as he lives, O dear one. (3)

8.9.m:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to Gaṅgā, who flows along three paths, / situated in the northeast from Saṅgāleśa, at a distance of seven bow-lengths. (1)
In it, the aquatic fish are constantly three-eyed, O dear one. / Even in the Kali age they are seen; truly, truly this is spoken by me. (2)
Having bathed in it, O great goddess, one is liberated from the five great sins. (3)
Sūta said:
Hearing those words of his, the chaste daughter of the mountain was astonished. / She said to that deity whose crest is the crescent moon, O best of the twice-born: (4)
Pārvatī said:
How did Gaṅgā who flows along three paths arrive there? / How did the aquatic fish become three-eyed, O Śiva? (5)
Tell this in detail, if I am dear to you, O lord. (6)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O goddess, I shall explain if you ask me, O auspicious one. / "They are believers and faithful"—such is my opinion. (7)
When Mahādeva was cursed by the seers filled with wrath / and enveloped by the darkness of ignorance on some occasion, (8)

8.9.m:
Having reached Saṅgāleśvara in Prabhāsa, which destroys sins, / they constantly performed austerity after installing Maheśvara. (17)
Then, after a long time, all those eminent sages, / through meditation on the three-eyed one though Maheśvara was not visible, (18)
attained three-eyedness, steadfast in austerity and rich in asceticism. / Looking at one another with the suspicion of being the three-eyed one, (19)
they praised [each other] with various hymns, believing each to be Maheśvara. / Realizing that by meditation on the god they had acquired three eyes, (20)
they performed fierce austerity and worship of the trident-bearing god. / While they were performing austerity, Maheśvara, filled with compassion, (21)
said to all those sages: "Receive an excellent boon! / I am pleased, O best of sages, by your austerity and by your worship." (22)
The seers said:
"If you are pleased, O lord of the gods, deign to grant us a boon: / Bring Gaṅgā swiftly for our ritual ablution, O Hara! (23)

8.9.m:
Having performed the ablution in it, we who committed an offense against you / out of ignorance will attain purity on the earth's surface." (24)
Īśvara said:
"You are makers of purity, and the purifiers of purifiers. / Yet I shall bring Gaṅgā for the gratification of your mind. (25)
Your possession of three eyes arose from your purity, O best of sages." / Having spoken thus, Śambhu, with eyes motionlessly fixed in meditation, (26ab)
remembered in an instant Gaṅgā, filled with schools of fish. (26cd)
The moment she was remembered, the divine Gaṅgā who flows along three paths / burst through the ground and arrived there, filled with schools of fish. (27)
And when the auspicious Gaṅgā accompanied by fish was seen by the seers, / those fish, as soon as they were seen, became three-eyed. (28)
Īśvara said:
"By the darśana of you, O brahmins, they have attained three-eyedness. / This is an illustration and a demonstration for all worlds." (29)

"O Mahādeva, by your grace, may the entire offspring of the fishes in this pool / always possess three eyes in age after age.
Whichever man, having come to this pool, performs ritual ablution, / and gives gold, cows, cloth, and sesame seeds to a brahmin,
especially on the new-moon day, may he become three-eyed!"
Having said, "So it shall be," Hara indeed vanished.
All the brahmins, filled with satisfaction, went to Mahodaya.
This excellent māhātmya of the Gaṅgā has been told to you, O goddess; / heard, it alleviates sins and grants the fruit of all desires.

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to the one situated to the east of it, / named Nāradāditya, which destroys old age and poverty,
three hundred bows to the west of Mūlacaṇḍīśa.
Having propitiated the sun, the stealer of waters, O goddess, Nārada,
his body freed from old age, was instantly restored [to youth].
The goddess said:
How did Nārada, the best of sages, attain old age? / How was the sun propitiated? Tell me this, O Śaṃkara.

Sāmba said:
"What need is there for seers of controlled self to have salutations?
And through their blessing, loss of austerity arises.
The inherent nature of sages does not exist in you in the slightest, O Nārada,
son of Brahmā! What more need be said than this?

Without a fight you have no happiness, no happiness without quarrel; / of whatever kind it may be, even dispute is ever dear to you!

8.9.m:
Ritual ablution, twilight prayer, recitation, oblations, libations to ancestors and gods—
Nārada does one thing, while brahmins do another!
Since you, arrogant on account of your perpetual youth, curse me, / therefore you too, O brahmin seer, shall be afflicted with old age!"
Thus cursed then, O goddess, Nārada, the best of sages, / in a solitary, clean spot, free of thorns and bones,
sat upon an excellent seat covered with a black antelope skin.
Having installed on the delightful bank of the Ṛṣitoyā,
O great sage, a beautiful image of the sun that destroys all poverty, / he praised Āditya, the dispeller of darkness, with various hymns:
"Salutations to you whose nature is the Ṛg[veda]; salutations to you who dwell in the realm of the Sāmaveda hymns! / Salutations to you whose body is pure knowledge, whose darkness is shaken off!
..
To you whose nature is pure light, bodiless, immaculate-souled, / most eminent, most worthy, the Supreme Self of all!
Salutations to the form of bliss whose nature pervades the whole universe, / the pure source of all causes, the resting place of minds endowed with knowledge!

Salutations to you who are the form of all, whose form is ungraspable by light! / Salutations to you, the maker of splendor, and salutations to the maker of day!"
Īśvara said:
As he was thus praising, before his mind, O ruler of gods, / the eternal eye of the universe manifested.
Supremely pleased, he spoke to Nārada, the best of sages.
Sūrya said:
"Choose a boon, O brahmin seer, which rests in your heart; / pleased, I shall grant it to you, even if it were very hard to attain."
Nārada said:
"Endowed with youthful age, my body has become afflicted with old age; / by your favor may I be [restored], O god, if you are pleased, O maker of day!
Whichever human sees you on a Sunday during the seventh lunar day, / may he have no fear of disease, by your grace, O dispeller of darkness!"
Īśvara said:
Having said, "So it shall be," the sun vanished.
Thus this entire māhātmya has been told to you, O goddess,
of the god Nāradāditya, which destroys all sins.

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to the unsurpassed Sāmbāditya / to the north of it, which destroys all sins,
..
where Sāmba, having performed austerity and propitiated the maker of day, / obtained a handsome body by the grace of the thousand-rayed one.
When the son of Jāmbavatī was cursed in anger by his father, / he then propitiated the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu,
for mitigation of the curse, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī.
Becoming cheerful-faced, Viṣṇu said to him:
"Go to the Prabhāsa kṣetra, to the unsurpassed portion belonging to Brahmā, / on the delightful bank of the Ṛṣitoyā, adorned by brahmins.
There I, in the form of Sūrya, shall grant you a boon, O son."
Having been addressed thus at that time by Viṣṇu, the mighty lord,

Having gone there, the son of Hari said these words / to those brahmins who dwelt in the high place, as many as were there:
Sāmba said:
"This is indeed the portion of Brahmā in the excellent sacred field of Prabhāsa. / The brahmins who dwell here are considered the foremost on earth.
At your word, O brahmins, I shall worship Sūrya. / This place was previously assigned to me by Viṣṇu."

8.9.m:
"Attainment will be yours, O Sāmba; worship the Sun!" / Thus told then by the brahmins, he approached Prabhākara.
Sāmba, son of Jāmbavatī, worshipped constantly. / And seeing him steadfast in austerity, the greatly compassionate Viṣṇu,
filled with affection for his son, reflected thus: / "Just as Rudra bestows sovereignty, and Viṣṇu bestows liberation,
and the lord of gods, worshipped with sacrifices, is remembered as the granter of heaven; / just as water combined with earth and ashes brings purification,
just as fire has the nature of burning, and the lord of the gaṇas is the remover of obstacles,
and just as the daughter of Brahmā bestows spontaneous speech upon men, / even so there is no god other than the Sun who bestows health.
Though worshipped in many ways, that pure god Bhāskara / does not grant the boon because of my curse."

8.9.m:
Having reflected thus, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed Janārdana, / assumed the form of Sūrya, pleased with him. / He who is known as Apara-Nārāyaṇa stood in his very presence; / then Viṣṇu, visible to the eyes, having the form of Sūrya the Sun,
exceedingly pleased, the giver of boons to those of meritorious deeds, spoke:
"Enough with your distress, O Sāmba! Why do you practice austerity? / I am pleased, O son of Hari; choose a boon, O you of noble vows!"
Sāmba said:
"By your grace, may I become pure, my body freed from leprosy, / O god of gods, O visible ornament of the sky!
Remaining in this delightful place, be ever present!"

Sūrya said:
"Now your body will become pure, O Sāmba! / But that man who, having come here on the seventh day of the fortnight that falls on a Sunday,
intent upon fasting, remains keeping vigil at night,
the eighteen types of leprosy and sinful diseases / will never arise in the family of that noble soul.

8.9.m:
A man who performs a ritual ablution and, endowed with devotion and self-restrained, / worships on Sunday Sāmbāditya of great splendour,
that man becomes free of disease, wealthy, and blessed with sons.
To the east of that very place, slightly toward the northeast, / is a holy pool that removes sins, filled with clear water.
A wise man who bathes there according to rule, performs śrāddha, / feeds brahmins, and worships Sāmbāditya,
with his soul abundant in all desires, is honoured in the world of the Sun."
Thus ends the three hundred and sixth chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Sāmbāditya', in the first [sub-section], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
East of Sāmbāditya, situated slightly toward the southeast, / is the one named Apara-Nārāyaṇa, than whom there is none higher on earth.

8.9.m:
Indeed, for Sāmba's sake, O ruler of gods, Sūrya, possessing the nature of Viṣṇu, / assumed another form having the form of Viṣṇu and granted the boon.
Because of that, Viṣṇu was formerly known by the name 'Apara'. / On the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, according to rule,
one should worship the lotus-eyed Lord there who has the nature of Sūrya. / He is freed from sins and prospers with all desired objects.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventh chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Apara-Nārāyaṇa', in the first [sub-section], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
East of that Nārāyaṇa, situated slightly toward the northeast, / is that which is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mūlacaṇḍīśa,
where formerly our liṅga was felled by the seers, O beloved, / their eyes red with anger, O goddess, and it attained the state of Mūlacaṇḍīśa.

8.9.m:
That original manifestation of the liṅga, O goddess, was brought down through the anger of the seers. / Whichever seers were residing there in the Devadāru forest,
in the course of time, O great goddess, I went there / to test them, O goddess, and thereupon they became enraged.
Then I was cursed, O ruler of gods, and they caused the falling of my liṅga.
The Goddess said:
"How did these twice-born men come to have their good disposition destroyed by anger? / Tell me this, for my curiosity is great."
Īśvara said:
"Formerly, O goddess, having assumed the form of a ḍiṇḍin in the Dāruka forest, / I wandered naked begging for alms in the holy hermitage of the seers. / Seeing me begging in the hermitage, all those wives of the seers
fell under the sway of desire, abandoning their dear [husbands] on all sides.
Beholding him with erect liṅga, wearing a crown of matted locks,
begging alms, his limbs smeared with ashes, like another Kāma, / [the seers said:] 'All our wives have been perturbed by this ḍiṇḍin!

Therefore, we shall utter a curse!' So those seers spoke then. / Then, taking water for a curse and having meditated, those rich in austerity [said]:
'May the liṅga of this one, which is seen ever erect, fall down!' / When this was spoken, my liṅga fell there in that temple.
It is renowned in the three worlds by the name Mūlacaṇḍīśa. / Seeing that liṅga fallen, their minds stricken with anger,
those men rich in austerity began once more to kill the ḍiṇḍin.
Some with kusa grass cushions in hand, others holding water-pots, / and others seizing their sandals, ran behind him.
And Ḍiṇḍi, vanishing from sight, said to you of slender waist: / “Look at these ascetics, their minds afflicted by wrath!
For this reason, O sinless goddess, at your word / I did not bestow grace upon those wrathful ascetics.”
Meanwhile, those sages, not seeing Ḍiṇḍi, / all went, devoid of joy, to see the god, the Grandfather [Brahmā].

8.9.m:
Having seen him, the lord of gods, Virañci, free from feverish distress, / bowing with their heads, all the seers spoke plainly:
“O Lord, there is an ascetic in the form of Ḍiṇḍi / who entered to beg alms, truly to ruin our wives.
He was cursed by us, the wicked one, and his liṅga was felled. / When it fell down, ours likewise fell down.
He departed on that account; and since that liṅga fell, / we all remain devoid of joy. Tell us the reason for this!”
Brahmā said:
“This great deed done by you was shameful, / since full of envy you attempted to kill Rudra of exceedingly handsome form!
Asura, Dānava, divine, Yakṣa, and Kiṃnara women, / and Vidyādhara, Gandharva, and charming Nāga maidens—
setting aside these choice women, [could he find] in yours...
pleasure? Do you not realize at all, O twice-born? / She who is the mistress of the three worlds, endowed with the utmost beauty—

leaving her, how could he take pleasure in the wives of sages? / For Rudra was requested by her: ‘Show grace to the seers.’

By this curse, a great fault is born of you. / Unless worshiped, the liṅga that has sunk down will not attain elevation.”
When this was spoken by the god, the brahmins said to the Grandfather: / “Where can he be seen by us? Tell us as it really is!”
Brahmā said:
“He resides in the form of an elephant, stationed at the hermitage of Kubera. / Going there and approaching him, propitiate the wielder of the Pināka.”
Hearing this speech of his, all those ascetics, delighted in mind, / set out at once in their tens of millions,

thinking of the auspicious region, in order to see that elephant-formed / Rudra, residing in the hermitage of Kubera, described by the Grandfather.
Knowing the ascetics to be thirsty, their throats parched with hunger, / Gaurī, taking cow-milk, stood before them out of compassion.
[Folio] 176b
Bearing on her head a braid of hair dark, curled, glossy, and long like a female serpent, / Gaurī was accompanied by cow-milk.
She said to all those sages: “What has been brought by me from the mountain / is cow-milk fragrant like kapittha fruits, resembling nectar.”
Addressed thus by her, the brahmins said to the wide-eyed goddess: / “Having bathed, all of us will drink the cow-milk brought by you.”
Then, having heard that, an excellent sacred ford for bathing / was made by the goddess: a delightful pool filled with hot water.
Having bathed there, all of them were freed from great fatigue. / Having performed their daily rituals, they approached to drink the cow-milk.

Having drunk, they attained satisfaction; / freed from hunger, thirst, and fatigue, they stood as if reborn.
Then with composed minds they realized: “This is no cowherdess; / this Gaurī has come for the sake of bestowing grace upon us.”
Bowing with their heads, they all said to her of slender waist: / “O Umā, tell us where we may see Rudra stationed at once?”
Thus addressed, she said to those great-souled ones: “Behold that great elephant! / Having assumed an elephant’s state, he roams about, possessed of great strength.
..
He should be taken hold of at ease by you through your own devotion.” / Hearing that word of hers, the twice-born assembled in one place;
purified, with an inner self imbued with devotion, in order to see that elephant. / Where the brahmins stood together in one place, there is a most auspicious sacred ford,

Then setting out from there, desiring to see the great elephant, / abandoning their small water-pots, girding up their own selves,

Stationed in that place, the elephant-formed one of great strength / stands in the world as Unnata, in the form of Gaṇanātha.
..
Assuming the form of Ḍiṇḍi, Rudra said to those rich in austerity: / 'Whatever service I must perform for you, let it be spoken here.' 54.

Pardon, O lord of the gods of gods, what was done by those of foolish mind. / By your grace, O lord of gods, be gracious [unto us].' 56.

Īśvara said:
'Caṇḍī is called the Goddess, and I am known as her Lord. / The liṅga is known as its root, because it fell here. 59.
Therefore it shall become renowned as Mūlacaṇḍīśa. / Whatever merit is generated by hundreds of large stepwells, wells, and tanks, 60.
that merit comes from the darśana of the liṅga. Whatever fruit of merit one might obtain by giving the entire cosmos, 61.
that merit one obtains, O goddess, from the darśana of Mūlacaṇḍīśa. / There sixteen gifts should indeed be given by the best of men. 62.
All that which was spoken by me will thus come to pass, O best of the twice-born! / Go to the Dāru forest, O brahmins, all you who are rich in austerity!
All directed by me, go to the Dāru forest, O twice-born!' 63.
Then, having received my great, highly auspicious word, all the sages rejoiced;
and having gone to that Dāru forest, O Maheśvarī, those rich in austerity again performed severe austerity. 64.

8.9.m:
For this reason, O goddess, the liṅga named Mūlacaṇḍīśa, / adorned with the crescent moon, removes the sin of men. 65.
Because of the pail, by the gift of milk to the thirsty sages, / the supreme removal of fatigue that was performed by you, O goddess,
from that, a pool named Taptodaka came to be on the surface of the earth. 66.
Whoever bathes in the water of Ṛṣitoyā and worships Caṇḍīśa / becomes fierce on earth, a sovereign lord of the worlds. 67.
Thus in brief has the māhātmya of Lord Mūlacaṇḍīśa / been proclaimed to you, O goddess; heard, it destroys sin. 68.

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to Hari Gopālasvāmin, / situated to the east of Caṇḍīśa, at a distance of twenty bows. 1.
He pacifies all sins and destroys hosts of poverty. / Having seen and worshipped him, especially in the month of Māgha,
having performed worship and a vigil there, one goes to the supreme state. 2.
Thus ends the three hundred and eleventh chapter, named 'Description of the Māhātmya of Gopālasvāmin Hari', in the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the first [sub-section] in the seventh [section], Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 311.
Īśvara said:
To the north of that, O dear one, at eight bows, / one should see the Sun, Bakulasvāmin, who destroys sorrow. 1.

8.9.m:
A person should keep vigil on a Sunday on the seventh lunar day; / he obtains all desires and is glorified in the realm of the Sun. 2.
Thus ends the three hundred and twelfth chapter, named 'Description of the Māhātmya of Bakulasvāmin', in the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the first [sub-section] in the seventh [section], Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 312.
Īśvara said:
To the north-west from that, situated at sixteen bows, / is the one named Uttarārka, who brings immediate conviction.
One is indeed freed from all diseases by performing the Nimba-saptamī [observance]. 1.
Thus ends the three hundred and thirteenth chapter, named 'Description of the Māhātmya of Uttarārka', in the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the first [sub-section] in the seventh [section], Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 313.
Īśvara said:
Now, to the south-east of Devakulā at a distance of one gavyūti, / situated on the shore of the ocean, is the charming, unsurpassed Ṛṣitīrtha. 1.

8.9.m:
There, seers in the form of stone are situated even today; / they are seen in human form, O goddess, destroying all sins. 2.
There, on the new moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, [the opportunity] is not attained by base men / to offer rice balls and especially [take] a ritual ablution, endowed with faith.
At the confluence of the Ṛṣitoyā, a ritual ablution and funeral rite are very hard to attain; / the foremost sages praise the gift of cows there.
Moreover, one should give food to brahmins according to one's ability. // 4
Thus ends the three hundred and fourteenth chapter, entitled 'Description of the Māhātmya of the Ṛṣitīrtha Confluence' in the Mūlacaṇḍīśa-māhātmya, in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetra-māhātmya, in the seventh [section], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand [verses]. // 314

Then, O great goddess, one should go to the goddess Kaṇṭakaśoṣiṇī, / situated north of Devakula and south of Unnata. // 1
I shall tell of her origin; listen with single-minded attention, O dear one. / To the south of Unnata, the best of the twice-born were sacrificing: // 2
Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Bharadvāja, and Kaśyapa, / Kaṇva, Maṅki, Sāvarṇi, and likewise Jātūkarṇya, // 3
Vatsa, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, / Manu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Viṣṇu, Śātātapa, Parāśara, // 4
Śāṇḍilya, Kauśika, Gautama, Gārgya, / Dālbhya, Śaunaka, Śākalya, and Gālava, // 5
Jābāli, Mudgala, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka, / Viśvāmitra, Śatānanda, Jahnu, and Viśvāvasu. // 6
These and other sages were sacrificing with diverse sacrifices, / having constructed an enclosure for sacrifice on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā, // 7

8.9.m:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the excellent Unnatasthāna, / on its northern side on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā.
This place, O great goddess, I granted by force to the brahmins, / complete with all its boundaries, guarded by the attendants of Caṇḍī.
The goddess said:
How did it get the name Unnata, O best of the gods? / Why was it granted by you by force, and what are its boundaries?
Tell me all this in brief, not in great detail.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O goddess; I shall tell the sin-destroying story, / hearing which a mortal, O goddess, is freed from all sins.
All this reason for naming the place was told formerly, / at the third pool of Brahmā, which indicates the summary of creation.
Even so, I shall tell you in brief. Listen, O Pārvatī.
Where the liṅga was raised up again at that great rise, / that site, the best of places, is called Unnata ("elevated").

8.9.m:
Or because the eastern gate of the Prabhāsa [field] is elevated (unnata), / that site, the best of places, is called Unnata.
Or where the great seers became exalted (utkṛṣṭa) through learning and austerity, / that site, the best of places, is called Unnata.
When at the temple the brahmins propitiated the Great God / named Mūlacaṇḍīśa and reached that great height again,
the great seers performed austerities for sixty thousand years, / meditating on Maheśāna, the supreme, who has no beginning or end.
While they, numbered in millions, were performing austerities, O Pārvatī, / on the delightful, pure, sin-destroying bank of the Ṛṣitoyā,
having assumed the form of a mendicant, I went there once again, O spirited lady.
I was then recognized, O fair-faced lady, by all those ascetics there, / who saw the three times and were free from faults and passion.
The moment he was seen by the brahmins, Maheśvara ceased [his wandering]. / Saying, "Where are you going, O known Lord?" the twice-born followed him.

8.9.m:
As the sages were coming, crying, "O Lord! O Lord!", / running and illuminating the ten directions with their austerity,
179a
they saw only the liṅga; they did not see Maheśvara.
And whoever among them saw the liṅga named Mūlacaṇḍīśa, / all those sages then went to heaven along with their bodies.
When heaven was seen to be overflowing by the performer of a hundred sacrifices, / and other sages, radiant with austerity, were arriving in the same way,
Śatakratu, taking advantage of this interval, arrived on the surface of the earth / and covered the liṅga with his thunderbolt.
Eighteen thousand sages of celibate vows / stood there, but they could not see that unsurpassed liṅga.
Śakra, accompanied by his thunderbolt, was suddenly seen. / Before they could utter a curse, Purandara vanished.
Seeing them filled with anger, the Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, / comforting the sages, spoke to them with sweet words:

8.9.m:
"Why are you agitated, O best of the twice-born, who are ever devoted to peace? / Becoming cheerful in countenance, let my words be heard.
Why is heaven esteemed so highly by you, who are endowed with knowledge? / Where some are called the Vasus, and others the Ādityas,
and some are designated as the Rudras, and others as the two Aśvins, / of whom one, Indra, is proclaimed as the ruler.
Since, when one's merits are exhausted, men fall from it, / heaven, being accompanied by such misery, is not desired by the wise.
For this reason, O brahmins, follow my command: / Accept a delightful city of great splendour for your dwelling.
Let the agnihotra fires be offered to, O twice-born, and the gods ever / worshipped with various sacrifices, and veneration of the ancestors performed.
Let hospitality be offered continuously, and likewise the study of the Vedas.
For those who do so daily, even without accumulations of knowledge, / liberation will come in the end by my grace, O chief of brahmins."

8.9.m:
The seers said:
"Unable to protect [possessions], with food conquered, endowed with austerity, / what would we do here with a city, desirous as we are of devotion to you?"
Īśvara said:
"Devotion to the Supreme Lord will always be yours. / Accept the delightful city and follow my words."
Having spoken thus, the Lord God, slightly closing his eyes, / remembered Viśvakarman, the foremost of all craftsmen.
As soon as he was remembered, Viśvakarman stood before him with joined palms: / "Command me, O Lord! I shall carry out your bidding."
Īśvara said:
"O Tvaṣṭṛ, let a beautiful, auspicious city be built for the brahmins."
Thus addressed, Viśvakarman, looking all around at the ground, / bowed down and spoke to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world:
"The land has been examined by me: a city is indeed not suitable here. / Here is the direct temple of the deity and the descent of the liṅga.
Ascetics must reside here; it is not suitable for householders.

8.9.m:
For three nights, or five nights, or seven nights, O Maheśvara, / for a fortnight, a month, a season, or up to half a year,
householders accompanied by sons and wives should dwell in a sacred ford.
When the master of a house dwells in a sacred ford beyond six months, / disrespect arises in him due to fickleness of mind.
Then all the householders fall from dharma."
Thus addressed at that time by that Viśvakarman, / the god Śiva praised his words and spoke to him again:
"The dwelling of brahmin householders here does not please me either. / Where the liṅga was raised up on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā,
there, O Tvaṣṭṛ, best of artisans, cause a city to be built."

8.9.m:
“This excellent and delightful place was built by Viśvakarma, / and it is said to have thousands of villages in all directions. / 46
The sacred region all around the city is known as Nagnahara, / extending eight yojanas in length and breadth. / 47
The region where Hara roamed naked at will, / that most holy country people call Nagnahara. / 48
To the east is noble Śāṅkarī, and to the west the Nyaṅkumatī, / to the north the Kanakanandā, and to the south its limit is the ocean.
The area situated within these [boundaries] is known as the Nagnahara region. / 49
Measuring eight yojanas in length and breadth, / this entire region, along with Unnata, has been described by me. / 7.1.319.50
Accept this excellent city! Be gracious, O best of the twice-born! / Here there will be both devotion and liberation; of this there is no doubt.” / 51

“The command of Īśvara, the Supreme Self, cannot be rendered futile. / Yet for those devoted to austerity and the agnihotra, who are adorned with the study of the Vedas, / 53

he will give you wealth when he is properly worshiped. / Durgāditya will always be the bestower of health. / 57

Consenting with ‘So be it’, he gave them the excellent city, / adorned with seven-storied palaces radiant as the moon, / 62
accompanied by various villages and bounded on all sides. / 63
Sūta said:
Having thus given the city to them, the god Maheśvara / saw Viśvakarma standing before him with folded hands. / 64
Viśvakarma said:
“Behold, O Mahādeva, the city resembling a [divine] city, / built by your grace, having ascended the golden platform!” / 65
Hearing the words of Viśvakarma, the Blessed Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, / ascended the platform together with all the great seers. / 66
He viewed the lovely city adorned with ramparts. / All the seers praised the destroyer of Tripura situated there; / 67
Mahādeva said to them: “Choose an excellent boon!” / 68

Addressed thus by them, the god has remained perpetually on this platform. / In the Kṛta age it was made of jewels, O goddess, and in the Tretā age of gold; / 70
in the Dvāpara age the platform is said to have been of silver, and in the Kali age made of stone. / Thus the god remained there under the name Sthalakeśvara. / 71
Mahādeva is always to be worshiped by the inhabitants of the Unnata place; / in the month of Māgha, on the fourteenth day, an all-night vigil is especially [meritorious] there. / 72
Thus this great greatness of Unnata has been recounted, O goddess; / heard, it destroys the sins of men and grants the fruit of all desires. / 7.1.319.73

“And to the east of that, situated slightly towards the southeast, / is a pair of most sacred liṅgas established by Viśvakarma. / 1
When Tvaṣṭṛ arrived there to build the city, / he installed Mahādeva, and then constructed the city. / 2
And having built the delightful city by the power of this liṅga, / another liṅga was installed by that Viśvakarma. / 3
At the beginning of an undertaking and at the end of an undertaking, on a journey, at a marriage, [the construction of] a house, and the like, / by worshiping the pair of liṅgas one attains success instantly. / 4
Therefore, with every effort, with perfumes, nectar-like juices, and waters, / and with diverse offerings of food, O goddess, one should worship the pair of liṅgas.” / 5

“Now I shall proclaim to you the secret, supreme place / that takes away all sins of the people who dwell in the Unnata place: / 1
the māhātmya of the foremost god Brahmā of unmanifest origin, / the god situated in the Unnata place in the form of a child,
by merely beholding whom one is released from all sins.” / 2
The goddess said:
“Tell me, how is it that Unnata is said to be in the form of a child? / In all other places, the Grandfather has the form of an old man. / 3
In what place does he abide there, and for what purpose did he go there? / How is he to be worshiped by the foremost brahmins, and on which lunar day? Tell [me] in order!” / 4
Īśvara said:
“To the west of the Ṛṣitoyā, and to the northeast of Sthalakeśvara, / is the supreme abode of Brahmā, like a second world of Brahmā. / 5”
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are always to be worshipped in Prabhāsa. / Stationed in the portion of Brahmā on the auspicious bank of the Ṛṣitoyā is Brahmā. 6

8.9.m:
In the portion of Rudra at Agnitīrtha, eternal Rudra is to be worshipped. / On the delightful Mount Raivataka, Hari Dāmodara is to be worshipped. 7
Entreated by Soma, the divine Grandfather assumed the form of a child; / and being eight years old, he arrived at this excellent, elevated place. 8
Having seen the best of the twice-born, the all-pervading Brahmā stayed in that place. 9
There is no god equal to Brahmā; there is no guru equal to Brahmā. / There is no knowledge equal to Brahmā; there is no austerity equal to Brahmā. 10
So long do they wander in saṃsāra overwhelmed by sorrow, grief, and fear, / as long as they do not become devoted to the eldest of the gods, the Grandfather. 11
Just as a creature's mind is deeply attached to the sphere of sense objects, / if it were thus fixed on Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? 12
The supreme lifespan is traditionally ascribed to Brahmā, and half of it has indeed passed. / For him stationed in the elevated place, the second [half] will now take place. 13
180b
When that Grandfather came from the world of Brahmā to the elevated place, / he was then said to be an eight-year-old in the form of a child. 14

Then, after a long time, the Day-maker, pleased with her, / spoke sweet words, a god to Durgā of great splendour:
"Choose a boon, O goddess of gods; I am pleased by your austerity." 3

Īśvara said:
In the northern quarter from it, slightly tending to the north-west, / one should see Vināyaka, the granter of all perfections. 1
He who was formerly described by me, O goddess, as my friend, the giver of wealth, / is the protector of treasures in the form of Gaṇanātha.
He is stationed in this place, O beloved, in order to grant perfections to people. 2
On the fourth day coinciding with a Tuesday, with eatables and foodstuffs along with modakas, / one should worship him according to rule, O goddess; his success shall surely be achieved. 3

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O Great Goddess, to the unexcelled Vināyaka / on the delightful bank of the Ṛṣitoyā, the remover of all obstacles. 1

Therefore, by every effort, for the sake of an unhindered pilgrimage, / Gaṇanātha should always be worshipped with flowers, incense, and the like. 3
And on every fourth lunar day, by all inhabitants of the city, / a great festival should be performed there for the attainment of the realm's welfare. 4

The presiding deity of this city is Bhairava bearing the form of Rudra. / On the new moon day and on the full moon day, one should cause a great worship to be performed. 2
A man who bathes at Mahodaya and beholds Mahākāla / becomes rich in wealth in the world for seven thousand births. 3
Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, named 'Description of the Glory of Mahākāla', in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh Prabhāsakhaṇḍa in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a collection of eighty-one thousand verses. 326

8.9.m:
Whoever bathes there according to rule and satisfies the ancestors and the gods, / has no fear of the fault born of accepting gifts. / 2
Mahodaya grants great joy even to the twice-born / who are addicted to accepting gifts and whose minds are attached to sensual objects;
even to them it gives liberation; therefore it is renowned as Mahodaya. / 3
Indeed, for its protection, to the north of Mahākāla, / the Mothers are appointed, O great goddess, stationed there.
Having bathed there first, a person should worship those Mothers. / 4
Thus, O goddess, I have declared the great fortune of Mahodaya, / which destroys all sins of mortals and grants liberation through ceremonial bathing. / 5
That sacred ford extends half a krośa in circumference all around; / this middle portion is of supreme essence and always dear to the sages. / 6

Īśvara said:
To the northwest of it stands the destroyer of sins, / richly called Saṃgameśvara, where the seers gathered. / 1
To the east of that very [place] is a small pool that destroys sin, / connected with the submarine fire, where Sarasvatī arrived. / 2
..
Having bathed in the pool, a person should worship Saṃgameśvara; / for a thousand births, along with Fortune, sons, and loved ones,
separation never occurs to him, O great goddess. / 3
He is freed from all sins committed from birth until death. / 4
Thus ends the three hundred twenty-eighth chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Saṃgameśvara', in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the Skandamahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses. // 328
Īśvara said:

To its northern quarter, at a distance of twelve bow-lengths, / stands Unnata, the lord of obstacles, who destroys all hindrances. / 2
[Folio 181b]
Duly worshipped on the fourth lunar day with fragrant scents, fruits, and sweetmeats, / he grants desired wishes; one becomes victorious in the three worlds. / 3
Thus ends the three hundred twenty-ninth chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Unnata-Vināyaka', in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the Skandamahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses. // 329
Īśvara said:
To the north of that Unnatasthāna, at [a distance of] three yojanas, / there is the Lord of Hot Water, where Tala was slain of old, / 1
the ruler of the Daityas, O goddess, by the mighty Viṣṇu / after fighting a war for a hundred years; then he became Talasvāmin. / 2
Having bathed in the hot pool, a person should worship Talasvāmin; / offering a ball of rice, one obtains the fruit of ten million pilgrimages. / 3

Then, O great goddess, one should go to the well-known Kālamegha; / to the east of it is the guardian of the sacred field, who has the form of a liṅga. / 1
He should be worshipped on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day by men with offerings; / he grants desired objects properly; he is a wish-fulfilling tree in the Kali age. / 2
Thus ends the three hundred thirty-first chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Kālamegha', in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the Skandamahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses. // 331

To the east of the pool, at twenty-five bow-lengths, / is stationed Goddess Rukmiṇī, the destroyer of all sins. / 2
Having bathed in the hot-water pool that destroys ten million killings, / one should then worship Goddess Rukmiṇī, the giver of gold;
for seven births, no ruin of the household occurs for women. / 3
Thus ends the three hundred thirty-second chapter, titled 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Rukmiṇī', in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the Skandamahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses. // 332

Seen, it calms all sins and brings all happiness. / Having bathed and offered a ball of rice on the new moon day, / 2
one brings satisfaction to the ancestors for a full hundred crores of kalpas. / Having worshipped the one named Durvāseśvara there according to rule, / 3

one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices and attains all desires. / There, many liṅgas were established by seers; / 4
having seen, touched, and worshipped them, one is freed from all misdeeds. / Thus this whole sacred field from beginning to end has been told to you in order, O goddess, / 5
from the west of Bhadrā to the east, in succession from the beginning. / Heard, it pacifies sins and grants the fruit of ten million sacrifices. / 6

Whatever merit one obtains, O goddess, at the eastern and western confluences of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, / that very merit one obtains at the confluence of the Bhadrā. // 11
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-third chapter, entitled 'Description of the Greatness of Piṅgeśvara and Bhadrā at Madhumatī' in the Greatness of Taptodakasvāmin, in the first [part,] the Greatness of Prabhāsakṣetra, in the seventh [section,] Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. // 333
Īśvara said:
O Lord, Lord of the gods of gods, who brings [beings] across the ocean of worldly existence, / I ask you with devotion out of some curiosity once again: // 1
Regarding what was told by you, O Lord, about the great majesty of Talasvāmin, / what was the cause there, O Lord, by which Tala was struck down? // 2
..
Who is this celebrated Tala? What was his valor, and to what was he devoted? / From what place did he arise, and how was he born? Tell me! // 3
Īśvara said:
Listen, O goddess; I shall declare the secret that destroys sin, / which has not been told to anyone. I shall tell it to you completely. // 4

8.9.m:
Even the gods do not know the cause of Tala's origin. / In ancient times, in the Kṛta age, O goddess, he was celebrated as Govinda. // 5
In the Tretā [age he was known as] the lord Vāmana, in the third as the lord Stuti, / and in the Kali age, O great goddess, he is proclaimed as Talasvāmin. // 6
Likewise, Taptodakasvāmin is another name of his, O beloved. / Now I shall fully declare the origin of Tala to you, O dear one. // 7
There was a Dānava named Mahendra, who bore a terrifying form. / For ten million years indeed, austerity was performed by him formerly, O beloved. // 8
Endowed with the power of austerity, he conquered the gods along with Indra. / Having conquered all the gods, then, in the course of time, he arrived. // 9
He requested a battle with me, a most terrifying one. / Thereupon a great battle took place, which caused the destruction of the cosmos. // 10
Then, out of wrath in the great battle, from my body, O fair-faced one, / a flame arose there; in the midst of it, that Tala came into being. // 11
By him was seen that Mahendra, roaring and resorting to a mountain cave. // 12

8.9.m:
'Why do you roar, O fool? Fight with me!' / When this was spoken there, O sovereign of the gods, a battle with him commenced. // 13
When the battle between the two, Tala and Mahendra, was engaged there, // 14
by Tala, endowed with the valor of Rudra and performer of mighty deeds, / powerful in wrestling, Mahendra was struck down. // 15
Then, seeing him fallen, that Tala was astonished. / Knowing him then to be lifeless, he danced out of joy. // 16
While he was dancing, all the stationary and moving beings / trembled, O shapely woman, due to his majesty and vigor. // 17
Then the earth, overcome by the burden and oppressed by Tala, [trembled], / and all the gods, demons, and mortals were terrified with extreme fear. // 18
All the mountains were agitated, and the great oceans were stirred up. / The trees met destruction, and the rivers abandoned their courses. // 19
The sun and other luminaries lost their brilliance and did not shine. / The three worlds were agitated on account of the power of Tala's dance. // 20

Then all the hosts of gods went to Rudra for refuge. / The event was reported as it happened; then Rudra said to them: // 21
'Tala cannot be slain by me, O gods, for he is established in the status of a son.' / Having spoken thus, [he directed them] to Hṛṣīkeśa, who resides in the Prabhāsa sacred field, // 22
who is known by the name Stutisvāmin, situated before Durvāsas, / established in the eastern part near the Prabhāsa sacred field, // 23
near the Taptodakuṇḍa: 'Go there, O gods! / For kalpa after kalpa, indeed, that Dānava is pierced by him alone.' // 24
When this was spoken, the gods then went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa. / There those gods went to where the lord of Taptodaka is. // 25
Seeing Nārāyaṇa there, the gods, filled with faith, / praised Janārdana, the god of gods, with supreme devotion: // 26
'O Vaikuṇṭha, protect us gods! We have been driven away by Tala, / who was born from the fiery energy of Rudra that arose from the anger of Mahendra. // 27

to your side, O Great God. Be our refuge, O deity!' // 28

the mighty-armed one, dear to the sacred field of Prabhāsa, made an effort. // 29
Summoning the Daitya then into the midst of the Prabhāsa sacred field, / he then fought a battle, O goddess, that caused universal dissolution. // 30
Then all the gods, surrounded by their own armies, / fought a battle with the Daitya, an exceedingly great one causing hair to stand on end. // 31
Then, seeing the Daitya, possessed of great strength and resembling a mountain, / [the Lord,] whose glances were restless and who had Garuḍa as his vehicle, said: // 32

Hearing Nārāyaṇa's words and raising his hand, the Dānava, / the Daitya having the luster of the Death-maker at the end of time, then rushed forward. // 34
..
Then a battle commenced between the two desiring victory over each other: / locking legs with legs and arms with arms, // 35
binding neck with neck and likewise belly with belly. / In the meantime, the gods became terrified. // 36
Then, overcome by distress, Viṣṇu remembered Hara. / In that instant, Rudra arrived, mighty in strength, [saying,] 'What shall I do?' // 37
Viṣṇu said:
I am exhausted, O Lord of the gods of gods, by wrestling, O Śaṃkara. / Create hot water here now to dispel my fatigue. // 38
Then in a mere moment I will kill the terrible Tala. // 39
Īśvara said:
That hot water which was created formerly by Umā at the beginning of the Kṛta age, O Kṛṣṇa, / was made there for the sake of dispelling the fatigue of the seers. // 40

Because of the efficacy of that Daitya's sin, it had become cold again. / Then, at the end of the kalpa, it was brought back to heat again. // 41
Having spoken thus to the god, Maheśvara then looked upon [him] / with his third eye alone, blazing with garlands of flames.
By that mass of flames the pool was enveloped in the four quarters; / thus it became the pool of hot water (Taptodakuṇḍa), renowned on the face of the earth.
Then the supreme body of Nārāyaṇa was washed here; / from that washing of the god, his exhaustion vanished.
Then, his heart delighted, the god, having properly remembered ten crores of sacred fords, / cast [them] there and bathed [in it], O fair-faced woman.
183a
Then a great battle took place with Tala, exceedingly terrifying; / he struck the Daitya Tala on the head with a blow of his fist.
..
When that tumultuous battle began, the worlds together with the earth trembled;
the gods were terrified, the directions did not shine, and the universe swooned, shrouded in great darkness.
The Siddhas were overwhelmed, saying: “May Hari, the destroyer of sins, bring peace to this universe!”

8.9.m:
“Save us!” O ruler of gods, thus cried the hosts of great seers and the frightened beings.
Then, in a wrestling bout, the Dānava was thrown down to the earth; / pressing down his throat with [his] foot, [he] tormented [him] with [his] sword.
..
Then the Daitya, his neck pinned down by Viṣṇu, laughed; / the lotus-eyed [god] said to him: “What is the reason for this laughter?
One feels joy at prosperity and becomes sorrowful at ruin; / this is the worldly saying; yours, Daitya, is the opposite!”
Thus addressed, the Daitya then replied to Janārdana: / “That supreme state which is attained through sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, through many kinds of Vedic studies,
through observances of constant fasting, through ablutions, gifts, recitations, and the like, / by pure [souls] united in yoga—
that supreme state of Viṣṇu has been attained by me even through an evil disposition!” / When this was spoken, the blessed Viṣṇu became intent on granting a boon.
He spoke supreme words to Tala, the lord of the Daityas: / “Choose a boon, O lord of Daityas, whatever resides in your mind!”

Hearing this word of Viṣṇu, the Dānava made a request: / “O upholder of the earth, act in such a way that my name endures in the world!
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, / whoever beholds you with concentrated devotion, may his sin be destroyed!”
Saying “So it shall be,” the god attained joy; / various drums sounded, and a shower of flowers fell.
Upon the head of Viṣṇu, O highly fortunate one, the worlds became at peace; / then all the hosts of gods, filled with joy, danced,
and, united in gladness, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, spoke:
“This sacred ford is a great sacred ford, destroying all sins, / removing the fatigue of Viṣṇu, purifying [even] the slaying of a brahmin and other [sins].
Nārāyaṇa is present there, and Śaṃkara is there as Bhairava / in the form of the guardian of the field, renowned as Kālamegha.
I shall declare the rule of pilgrimage to it: having gone there, a purified man / should remember Viṣṇu, who is renowned as Talasvāmin, O great goddess.

8.9.m:
One should praise Viṣṇu, O great goddess, with this verse beginning with ‘Idaṃ Viṣṇuḥ’, O dear one; / with the hymn beginning with ‘Sahasraśīrṣan’ one should perform libations and the like.
Having thus bathed according to rule and offered water of reception to Janārdana, / and worshipped [him] with fragrant flowers, garments, and floral unguents,
one should anoint [him] with honey, sugarcane juice, and saffron / mixed with camphor and uśīra, and joined with musk.
Afterwards one should wrap [him] in garments and offer excellent food offerings; / then a vigil should be kept, accompanied by listening to dharma.
A bull should be gifted there, along with gold and a pair of garments; / one should present them to a learned brahmin devoted to the Vedas.
Then, O spirited woman, one should fast on that day, / and behold Rukmiṇī, having bowed to Janārdana.
Having done this with devotion, a man obtains the fruit of [all his] births; / he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and gifts,

8.9.m:
and likewise he obtains the fruit of all sacred fords and vows; / he redeems his father’s family and his mother’s family as well.
183b
There will be destruction of all sins committed since birth; / neither sorrow, nor poverty, nor misfortune arises [for him]
for seven subsequent births, from the sight of Talasvāmin. / Whatever fruit is obtained by giving a thousand gold coins
to a brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, O goddess, one obtains by bathing in that pool.
Thus the excellent deed of Talasvāmin was heard in ancient times by hosts of Siddhas and great seers;
having heard of the power [manifested] in the presence of the god Tala, one attains all that is desired by the mind.
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, entitled “Description of the Greatness of Talasvāmin,” in the first [part], the “Greatness of Prabhāsakṣetra,” of the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

8.9.m:
Then one should proceed to the west, to the auspicious bank of the Nyaṅkumatī; / facing the southern direction stands a sacred ford of great splendour,
renowned as Śaṅkhāvarta, where there is a stone marked with diverse patterns, / self-manifest, O great goddess, reddish within and very beautiful.
Even today, when it is split open, bright red [colour] is seen right there; / for that is proclaimed as the field of Viṣṇu where Śaṅkha was slain in ancient times,
the stealer of the Vedas, O ruler of gods, by the all-powerful Viṣṇu. / The sacred ford named Śaṅkhodaka was formed [there], and it is seen to have the shape of a conch.
Bathing there, O goddess, a man is freed from the slaying of a brahmin; / even for a Śūdra, the status of a brahmin arises for seven births.
Having gone there first, one should then proceed to Rudragayā; / the gift of a cow must be given there by those who desire the full fruit of the pilgrimage.

8.9.m:
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, entitled “Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkhāvarta-tīrtha,” in the first [part], the “Greatness of Prabhāsakṣetra,” of the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the supreme sacred ford, Goṣpada, / where, having performed a śrāddha, a man [obtains] seven times the fruit of Gayā;
he obtains it without any doubt, if his faith is firm. (1)
Where, having performed a śrāddha, Pṛthu delivered his father, / the great lord named Vena, from a sinful womb, O great goddess. (2)
The goddess said:
In what place is that sacred ford situated, and what was its origin? / How was that King Vena delivered from a sinful womb? (3)
How does merit seven times that of Gayā arise there? / What is the procedure for the śrāddha, which mantras are used there, and who are the brahmins? (4)
This is my curiosity, O god; you should tell me properly. (4)
Īśvara said:

This secret, O goddess of the gods, which has been asked by you— / this sacred ford is not to be revealed in this sinful age, O beloved. (5)
Even so, out of love for you I shall explain it fully, O ruler of the gods. / One must not tell this to a sinner, nor indeed to one devoted to [dry] logic, (6)

and not far to the north of the dwelling of Nārāyaṇa. / In its midst, O great goddess, is the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, (9)

The ancestors, greatly terrified of hell, long for sons: / ‘The son who will go to Goṣpada, he will be our saviour!’ (12)
