8.9.m:
And when they see a son at Goṣpada, a festival takes place for the ancestors: (12)
‘Touching the water even with his feet, will he not give [an offering] to us? / May there be someone in our lineage who will give us a handful of water, (13)
having reached the sacred field of Prabhāsa, at the supreme sacred ford Goṣpada! (13)
May there be someone in our lineage who will once carefully perform a śrāddha / with the flesh of a rhinoceros, or else with black greens! (14)
May there be someone in our lineage who has offered a lamp at Goṣpada; / through that, there will be light for us lasting until the end of the kalpa!’ (15)
The ancestors have sons indeed in him who feeds a hundred at Goṣpada; / having stayed even for a single day, he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation. (16)
A man should personally offer a ball of food to his father and other [ancestors], and even to himself; / even with oil-cake and inguda-fruit, he would be freed through that, O fair-faced one. (17)
What is the use of knowledge of Brahman, what of yogas, what of dying in the recapture of cattle, / what of dwelling in Kurukṣetra, if he goes to Goṣpada? (18)

8.9.m:
Visiting the sacred ford once, dropping a ball of food once— / this is hard to attain; what then of constantly abiding in this sacred ford? (19)
That sacred ford is half a kośa [in extent], and its half-of-a-half is especially rare to attain; / performing a śrāddha within it, one obtains seven times the merit of Gayā. (20)
One who performs a śrāddha at Goṣpada is indeed freed from debt to his ancestors; / especially in the middle of the footprint, he delivers a hundred lineages. (21)
For one who has merely departed from his home to go to Goṣpada, / at every step there is a stair to ascend to heaven for the ancestors. (22)
The offering of a ball of food is prescribed with milk-rice, with honey, / with roasted barley meal, with cake, with sacrificial boiled rice, or with rice grains and the like. (23)
..
He who offers balls of food in the cattle-pasture, of the size of a śamī leaf, / or with edible roots, bulbs, and fruits, leads his ancestors to heaven. (24)
The fruit that a man obtains by offering a ball of food at Goṣpada / cannot be spoken by me even in hundreds of crores of kalpas. (25)

8.9.m:
Now, therefore, I shall declare in full the auspicious rules of pilgrimage; / and likewise listen, endowed with complete faith, to the pilgrimage procedure: (26)
If a man should go to the sacred ford desiring the fruit of a śrāddha at Gayā, / the wise man should undertake the pilgrimage according to that kind of rite. (27)
Celibate, becoming pure, restrained in hands and feet, / faithful, believing, pure of heart, the wise man should then go to the sacred ford. (28)
At that sacred ford, a man should not have contact with an unbeliever; / equipped with all accessories, provided with materials worthy of a śrāddha, (29)
accompanied by the virtuous, keeping Gayā in mind, he should go to the sacred ford. (29)
A twice-born who goes in this manner, abstaining from accepting gifts, / obtains at every step the fruit of an horse sacrifice, without doubt. (30)
Having bathed there in the Nyaṅkumatī for success and for the liberation of his ancestors, / and having bathed, he should duly perform the libation of water for the gods and others: (31)
184b
‘From Brahmā down to a clump of grass, gods, seers, manus, and men, / and all ancestors, maternal grandfathers and mothers, may they be satisfied!’ (32)

8.9.m:
Having thus offered libations according to rule, and having performed the fire offering and other rites, / a man should perform the śrāddha with balls of food according to the rules stated in the manual, (33)
having invited brahmins there who know the scriptures and are free of faults. / Thus having performed the worship, he should recite this mantra: (34)
‘Kavyavāh, Agni, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman, / the Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads, and Somapas, the ancestral deities— (35)
may the highly blessed ones come here, protected by you! (35)
And whoever are my ancestors, born in the family as kinsmen, / I, the giver of balls of food to them, have arrived here, O forefathers!’ (36)
Having said this, O great goddess, he should recite this mantra: (37)
‘Father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, / mother, paternal grandmother, and great-grandmother, (38)
maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather: / the ball of food given by me to them—may it stand inexhaustible!’ (39)

‘Om, homage to the Sun, the sustainer, who has the forms of the Sun, Mars, and the Moon.’ / Having thus bowed and worshipped, he should then recite this praise: (40)
There, near Goṣpada, with well-boiled sacrificial porridge, / he should offer the balls of food with mantras for his ancestors and for the helpless ones. (41)
Those who have died in our lineage and have attained no destiny, / and those who have gone to Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra—
for their deliverance, I offer this piṇḍa. // 42
Those who are undergoing many torments, who have gone to the worlds of ghosts— / for their deliverance, I offer this piṇḍa. // 43
Those who have been reborn as animals, and those who are insects or reptiles, / or those who dwell in the womb of trees—to them I offer this piṇḍa. // 44
Those undergoing countless torments, who have been led away by Yama's chastisers— / for their deliverance, I offer this piṇḍa. // 45
Those who were kin, those who were not, and those who were kin in another birth— / may all of them attain satisfaction forever by this piṇḍa. // 46

Whichever of my ancestors exist in the form of ghosts— / may all of them attain satisfaction forever by this piṇḍa. // 47
The ancestors and kinsmen who dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, or on earth, / and those who died without rites—may this piṇḍa be for their liberation. // 48
Those who have died in the paternal line, and likewise in the maternal line, / and any other kin who have died among the relatives of preceptors and fathers-in-law, // 49
those in my lineage who have been deprived of piṇḍas, who were destitute of sons and wives, / and those who have missed funeral rites, those born blind, and those who are lame, // 50
the deformed, premature miscarriages, and those unknown or known in my lineage— / the piṇḍa offered by me, may it attend them inexhaustibly. // 51
May my ancestors be freed from ghosthood forever! / Whatever cow's milk mixed with honey, ghee, or milk-rice, // 52
may it attend [them] inexhaustibly from you at this sacred ford Goṣpada. / One should recite the sacred study there, and all the Purāṇas as well, // 53

and various hymns to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Rudra, / hymns to Indra, the Soma hymns, and the Pāvamānī verses according to one's ability, // 54

Having thus offered piṇḍas according to rule in the middle of the Nyaṅkumatī / at the excellent sacred ford Goṣpada, one should again recite this mantra: // 57

8.9.m:
The gift of a cow should be given there, as well as a black antelope skin, my dear, / on the Aṣṭakā days, during rites of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death. // 61
Here the śrāddha for the mother is performed separately; elsewhere, together with the husband; / but in the śrāddha of prosperity, [the offering] begins with the mother and others, and at Gayā it begins with the father. // 62
Just as at Gayā, the śrāddha should be performed right here by the best of men; / therefore this place was declared by Viṣṇu himself to be the Hidden Gayā. // 63
By giving perfumes one attains fragrance; good fortune comes from giving flowers; / from the gift of incense comes the attainment of kingship; radiance comes from the gift of a lamp. // 64 // / From the gift of a banner comes the destruction of sin; one who undertakes the pilgrimage attains the world of Brahmā. / Viṣṇu will indeed lead to the [highest] realm the ancestors of him who offers a śrāddha-piṇḍa. // 65
If one feeds even a single brahmin of commended vows there / at that great sacred ford Gopracāra, ten million have been fed. // 66

This holy [account] must not be told to a slanderer, nor to a sinner, / nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to an ill-wisher, nor ever to one without vows. // 69
It leads to heaven, brings fame, grants long life, brings prosperity, and is equal to the Veda. / Whoever, without envy, listens to this secret declared by the seers, // 70

8.9.m:
Seeing him afflicted and distressed, they indeed said, "Sit down (niṣīda)!" / From that, he became the Niṣāda, founder of a lineage, of immense might.
He also produced the Dhīvaras, born from the sin of Vena, / and others dwelling in the Vindhya mountains, as well as the Tuṃbaras and Khasas.
Born from Vena's sin, taking delight in unrighteousness, they increased. / Then the great seers once again [churned] Vena's right hand,
churning it furiously, like a fire-drill, filled with rage. / From that hand arose Pṛthu, resembling a blazing fire.
Since he was born from the broad palm (pṛthu) of his hand, he was therefore named Pṛthu; / he was resplendent in body, blazing like fire incarnate,
holding the Ajagava bow, arrows resembling venomous serpents, / carrying a sword for protection, and wearing radiant armor.
Upon his birth, O great goddess, all living beings / became exceedingly rejoiced, and Vena went to heaven.

Because he was born among the Sāman-singers, he is called a Māgadha. / When Bṛhaspati offered an oblation mingled
with an oblation meant for Indra, sacrificing unto Indra, from that [rite] he was born. / An error occurred therein, requiring an expiation in the rituals.
[Folio] 186a
Because the Teacher's oblation was mixed with and overwhelmed by the remainder-offering, / that alteration of caste arose through an inversion of high and low accent.
In that sacrifice, he was born from a kṣatriya source upon a brahmin woman. / Therefore, because of shared nature with what preceded, they are declared to share common duties.
For this middle duty of his essence is to live by serving kṣatriyas, / dealing with chariots, elephants, and horses, and, lowest of all, the practice of medicine.
The two were summoned there by the great seers to recount the deeds of Pṛthu. / All the sages said to them: "Let the king be praised!
For this ruler of the earth is indeed worthy on account of his deeds." / Then the sūta and the māgadha said to all those seers:

8.9.m:
"We two shall please the gods and seers by our proper duties; / but we do not know his deeds, nor his qualities and fame,
by which we might compose a eulogy for this radiant king, O twice-born." / But the two were directed by the seers: "Let him be praised for his future deeds!"
Whatever deeds the mighty Pṛthu accomplished later on, / those were sung and composed in verse by the praising sūtas and māgadhas.
Having heard their meaning, Pṛthu, lord of subjects, was highly delighted / and bestowed the coastal region (Anūpa) on the sūta, and the Magadha regions on the māgadha.
From that time forward, kings are praised by sūtas and māgadhas; / they are extolled with blessings by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
Seeing him, the subjects were exceedingly delighted, and the great seers said: / "This son of Vena has been appointed as your king, the provider of your livelihood."
Then the subjects rushed together to the illustrious son of Vena, / saying, according to the words of the great seers: "You are the ordainer of our livelihood!"

8.9.m:
Addressed thus by the subjects, wishing to secure the welfare of his subjects, / the mighty king took up bow and arrows and assailed the earth.
Then, terrified with fear of Vena's son, the earth assumed the form of a cow and fled. / Taking [his bow], Pṛthu pursued that fleeing cow.
Having gone to various worlds, beginning with the world of Brahmā, out of fear of Vena's son, / she saw Vena's son standing in front of her, bow raised in hand, / equipped with blazing, sharp arrows endowed with radiant splendor, / endowed with great yoga, high-souled, and invincible even to the immortals.
Finding no protection, she surrendered to Vena's son alone. / With hands folded in reverence, the goddess who is ever worthy of worship by the three worlds
spoke to him: "Do you not see that killing a woman is unrighteous? / And how will you sustain your subjects without me, O king?
The worlds rest in me, O king; this universe is sustained by me. / Know this, O ruler of the earth: without me, the subjects would perish.

8.9.m:
Therefore you ought not to kill me, if you wish to act for the good / of the subjects, O protector of the earth! Listen to these words of mine:
All undertakings commenced by proper means succeed. / Having killed me, O king, you will indeed not be able to protect the subjects.
I will become accommodating; cast away your anger, O one of great splendor! / For they say that females are not to be slain, even when born of animals.
When one sinful person of cruel deeds meets destruction, / and safety comes to many, in that case killing brings merit.
This being so, O protector of the earth, you ought not to abandon righteousness."
Hearing such words, the mighty king, / restraining his anger, the righteous one spoke this to the earth:

When one is killed, however, and many thrive in happiness, / then indeed, when that one is slain, there is no sin for him.

8.9.m:
Therefore, I shall slay you for the sake of the subjects, O earth, / if today you will not carry out my word, which is for the welfare of the world.
Having slain you today with an arrow because you turn away from my command, / having expanded myself here, I will sustain the subjects.
Therefore, relying on my word, O best of upholders of righteousness, / revive the subjects constantly, for you are certainly capable, there is no doubt.
Become indeed my daughter; in this way I shall restrain / this great arrow of terrible appearance that was aimed to slay you.”
Addressed thus, the great virtuous lady then answered Vainya:
“I will accomplish all this, O king, there is no doubt. / But provide me with a calf, so that I, loving [my young], may pour forth.
And make me level everywhere, O best of sustainers of all, / so that, flowing forth, I may cause milk to arise everywhere.”
Īśvara said:
Then Vainya shoved away the masses of rocks on every side / with the tip of his bow; by that the mountains were increased.

8.9.m:
In the past Manvantaras the earth was indeed like this; / by its inherent nature it had level and uneven places.
For in the previous creation the surface of the earth was not uneven, / nor was there any division into cities and villages,
no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade route.
In the earlier interval of Cākṣuṣa this was so, as tradition relates; / but in this interval of Vaivasvata, the origin of all this [took place].
Wherever there was any evenness of the ground whatsoever,
in those places the subjects always dwelt. / The food of the subjects was indeed fruits and roots,
and then [obtained] only with difficulty by them; so we have heard. / Beginning with Vainya, the origin of all this occurred in this world.
Appointing the lord Cākṣuṣa Manu as the calf, / Pṛthu then milked the crops from the earth with his own hand.

8.9.m:
The crops were indeed milked from this earth by Vainya, / having made Cākṣuṣa Manu the calf, into an earthen vessel.
By that food those subjects then constantly sustain themselves. / And it is heard that the earth was milked again by the seers.
Soma was their calf, and Bṛhaspati was the milker; / the vessels were the metres, Gāyatrī and the rest, in every respect.
Their milk was then austerity and the eternal Veda. / Then again by the hosts of gods, led by Puraṃdara,
it is heard that this earth was milked, taking a golden vessel. / Maghavan was the calf, and Savitṛ was the milker.
The milk is declared to be invigorating honey; by that the deities sustain themselves. / And it is heard that the earth was milked again by the ancestors,
taking a silver vessel, [milking] svadhā for imperishable satisfaction. / The powerful Yama Vaivasvata was their calf,

The two-headed priest of the daityas, the son of Diti, was the milker; / he milked the milk of māyā, which causes satisfaction for the daityas.
By that, all these asuras, knowers of māyā, endowed with great heroism, / even today live by māyā; that is their supreme strength.
And it is heard that it was milked by the nāgas, having made Takṣaka the calf, / taking a bottle-gourd vessel, [milking] the great poison as milk.
Vāsuki of great renown, the son of Kadrū, was their milker, / [the milker] of the nāgas and of the snakes everywhere, O great goddess.
By that the fierce, huge-bodied [serpents], full of poison, sustain themselves; / having that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their strength, that as their refuge.

The vessel was made of stone; by that the mountains are firmly established. / It is heard that the earth was milked again by the trees and climbing plants,
taking a palāśa vessel, [milking] the regrowth of cut and burnt [parts]. / The flowering śāla tree was the milker, and the plakṣa tree was the calf, O illustrious lady.
Yielding all desires, the earth, creator of beings, was milked.
She is the supporter, the ordainer, the holder, and the bearer of wealth. / She was milked for the benefit of the worlds by Pṛthu; so we have heard.
She was the foundation and origin of the world of mobile and immobile beings; / ending at the ocean, she became renowned as Medinī.
Formerly covered with the fat and flesh of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, / because she bears wealth, she is called Vasudhā.
Then, having been accepted by the wise King Pṛthu, son of Vena, / she attained the status of his daughter; therefore she is called Pṛthivī.

Extensive, divided, and adorned, the earth / was milked with effort by the king, garlanded with cities and mines.
Such was the power of that king, the son of Vena, the best of monarchs; / then he pleased the earth with righteousness.
From that pleasing, the word 'king' arose upon the earth. / Having obtained the kingdom, the son of Vena, that ruler, thought:
'My father was indeed most unrighteous, the destroyer of sacrifices and the like. / To what place has he gone? How may that place be known by me?
How should his rites be performed, slain as he was by the brahmins? / How might he attain a [good] destiny through the power of sacrifices, gifts, and rituals?'
[Folio] 187b
While he was reflecting thus, Nārada arrived there. / Giving him a seat and bowing down, he asked:
'O Blessed One, you know the good and evil of all the world. / My father was evil-conducted, a reviler of the gods and brahmins.

Slain by the vipras through his own deed, he went to the other world. / To what place has my father gone—to a chasm of hell, or to heaven?'
Then Nārada, having perceived it with his divine eye, said: / 'Listen, O mighty-armed king, to where your father dwells.
Here there is a land named Maru, devoid of water and trees; / in that terrible land is your father, O best of men.
Born among barbarians, afflicted with consumption and leprosy, / eating the leavings of barbarians, covered with worms and sores.'
Hearing that speech of the high-souled Nārada, / he cried out 'Alas, alas!' and fell down unconscious.
Afflicted with grief, he pondered: 'What should be done by me?' / As he thought thus, the thought arose in that noble soul:
'He is called a son in this world who protects his father.
How then may my father be freed from sin by me?' / Having reflected thus, he then inquired of Nārada:

'O Blessed One, all the conduct of my father has been described. / By what action may he attain liberation, O best of the twice-born?
Tell me—by vows, by gifts, by austerities, or by a pilgrimage to sacred fords?'
Nārada said:
'Go to the foremost sacred fords, O king, O ruler of men, / and having brought your father from that desert region to them,
where the gods are powerful and the sacred fords are pure, / go there, O great king, and undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords, O lord.
Know for certain that thus the liberation of your father will take place.' / Hearing that speech of the high-souled Nārada,
the king placed the burden of his kingdom on his minister and departed.
Having gone to the desert land, he saw him in the midst of barbarians, / overcome with terrible leprosy and consumption,
and the area for a gavyūti around was deserted, devoid of men. / Seeing this, the king, tormented [with sorrow], spoke these words:

'O barbarians, I am taking this diseased man to my own home; / there I shall make him free of sickness, if you agree.'
Recognizing that man to be filled with compassion, all those barbarians, / with their whole bodies bowed down, said: 'Take him quickly, O lord of the world!
By virtue of our good fortune, O master, you alone have come here.
The people afflicted by the foul smell have been made happy by you, O master!' / Then, having summoned men suitable for carrying a litter,
and having heard that compassionate word of the king, / they reached countless millions of sacred fords, beginning with Kedāra.
Wherever the son of Vena went, accompanied by Vena, / in that very place a great lamentation of the sacred fords was heard:
'Alas, fate! An enemy approaches to destroy us! / Where shall we go now?'—such was their repeated anxiety.
Even at the sight of him, uttering cries of 'Alas, alas!', / the sacred fords fled and the deities vanished instantly.

8.9.m:
Thus for three years the king undertook a pilgrimage to sacred fords, / but his liberation was not seen; then he fell into profound grief.
[Folio] 188a
Then the servants were sent forward to Kurukṣetra, of great splendor: / 'Perhaps even there his liberation from sin may happen.'
Taking the litter on their shoulders, they went to Kurukṣetra, O dear one; / having carried him there, lowering him at Sthāṇutīrtha, they went.
Then that king at midday, desiring to perform his ritual ablution with devotion, / and also for that father of his the sixteen gifts,
wishing to bestow them on the brahmins, full of faith and devotion, / then the wind in the sky spoke these words:
'Do not act rashly, my child! Protect the sacred ford with effort! / This man is completely surrounded by terrible sin;
his conduct was to revile the Vedas, and he is burdened with hundreds of slayings of brahmins. / This sinful man of wicked conduct will destroy the sacred ford!

8.9.m:
Do not destroy the sacred ford, O lord, for a great fault will occur.' / Hearing these words of the wind, afflicted with great grief,
tormented by sorrow, pained by the sorrow of his father, he said—
crying out again and again with arms raised, 'Alas, fate! / He is exceedingly enveloped by terrible sin,
since he cannot be made pure even by this sacred ford! / I shall perform an expiation for the sake of my father, no doubt.'
Hearing his words, showing immense compassion, / the sky-dwellers spoke again, their voice arising from the atmosphere:
"O king, best of rulers, cast off your sorrow and listen to our words, / by which a great destruction of sin may come to this father of yours. // 211
There is a greatly perfected sacred field known as Prabhāsa, / pacifying all sins and destroying heinous crimes. // 212
The reality of Brahmā, the reality of Hari, and thirdly the reality of Rudra, / [reside] right in that great sacred field, Prabhāsa, dear to Śaṃkara. // 213

8.9.m:
Whether related to Śakti, to the moon, to the sun, or to Sarasvatī, / or to Agni, or to Varuṇa, it is regarded as an unsurpassable sacred field. // 214
Whatever sacred fords and ancient sacred fields exist in the universe, / they will all come to Prabhāsa when the Kali yuga arrives. // 215
Eighty million and eight hundred million gaṇas belonging to Śaṃkara / reside there and protect the sacred field of Prabhāsa. // 216
This holy Sarasvatī is present everywhere indeed; / but in Prabhāsa she has five streams, hard to attain even for the gods. // 217
Her fifth stream is the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, / and situated in the midst of it is the sacred ford known as Goṣpada. // 218
In its middle is the Preteśilā, which grants liberation to the deceased spirits; / where twenty-eight crores of deceased spirits were previously liberated. // 219
It is a sacred ford granting liberation to sinners, remembered as the primordial Rudragayā; / thus it is renowned on earth in the Kali [age] by the name Goṣpada. // 220

8.9.m:
When the mothers of the world emerged from the churning of the milk ocean, / they came together with the gods near the sacred ford. // 221
There, the footprint of Nandā sank into the stone surface; / and seeing the stone marked with a hoof and marked with the area of a knee, // 222
all the gods were astonished and questioned the cow Nandinī: / 'O goddess, what is this footprint seen on the surface of the Pretaśilā?
Why has distress arisen, and why has our stumbling occurred?' // 223
Nandinī said:
188b
'O gods, this footprint of mine shines situated on the stone, / like a second lunar disc resting on the courtyard of the sky. // 224
..
From this day forth, O gods, throughout the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings, / it shall become renowned in the world by the name Goṣpada. // 225
Whatever person comes here and performs a ritual ablution and an ancestral rite, / his fruit, O gods, will be seven times that of Gayā. // 226
Neither the day of the week, nor the lunar mansion, nor the time is the determining factor there; / whenever the sacred ford is seen, that is equivalent to a thousand auspicious occasions. // 227

and the fifteenth of Kārtika, of Phālguna, and of Jyaiṣṭha: / these are the beginnings of the manvantaras, rendering what is given imperishable. // 235
On the third of Vaiśākha, on the dark [fifteenth] of Phālguna, / on the fifth of the month of Caitra, and likewise the final other one of that very month, // 236
on the bright thirteenth of Māgha, the seventh of Kārtika, / and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa—these seven are the beginnings of the kalpas. // 237

instantly vanished, like a lamp extinguished by the wind. // 238
Having witnessed this wonder, all the gods together with Indra, / the brahmin-seers, and the celestial seers sang a Purāṇic verse: // 239
'Ah, the māhātmya of the sacred ford, and the power of Nandā's austerity! / By an ancestral rite offered only once, the fruit is seven times that of Gayā.' // 240
Having spoken thus, the gods then performed the ancestral rites and other ceremonies; / they attained the fruit as declared, which had previously been spoken by Nandinī. // 241

8.9.m:
In this manner, O sovereign king, go quickly indeed to Goṣpada; / having performed the ancestral rites and other rites there, you will obtain the desired fruit. // 242
This father of yours, O king, is regarded as the foremost among sinners; / he cannot be fully redeemed by hundreds of other sacred fords, except Goṣpada. // 243
Therefore go, great king; do not make delay." / Having heard this, the king then went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa. // 244
Placing in front the brahmins residing in that place, who were experts in the māhātmya of the sacred ford, / the great king went to the river Nyaṅkumatī. // 245
By them the sacred ford was shown to the king, the footprint situated on the Pretaśilā; / and seeing that immaculate sacred ford, his eyes opened wide with astonishment.
He constructed pits, altars, and pavilions for the success of the sacrifice. // 246
Then the sacrifice was commenced according to the rules, with abundant priestly gifts; / his ancestors appeared before his eyes, shining with the brilliance of fire. // 247
Then, having taken recourse to faith through ancestral rites and sacrifices of great prosperity, / those ancestors, being gratified, spoke these words to the best of kings: // 248

8.9.m:
189a
"You are fortunate, O king, you are virtuous, and we are even more fortunate through you, / since we have been delivered by you here in this sacred ford through an ancestral rite." // 249
Having spoken thus, all those ancestors together with Vena / mounted excellent aerial chariots and went to the abode of heaven. // 250
As he was departing, Vena said to that broad-chested king: / "O king, for four births, and in another birth, // 251
I was a leper, a sinner of bad conduct, and an eater of the remnants of outcasts. / Completely freed from sin, I now go to the abode of heaven." // 252
Therefore go, O fortunate one, and enjoy your kingdom for a long time. / All that a son ought to do has been done for you.
Having heard this, the king then rejoiced together with his kinsmen. / He gladdened the brahmins with gifts of land, gold, and other riches.
There was nothing in this world that the king did not give away there, / having seen the power of the sacred ford and the direct sight of his ancestor.

8.9.m:
Having done this, the king returned to his own abode. / Having enjoyed the whole earth, after death he attained heaven.
Such is the power of that sacred field Prabhāsa, which destroys sins, / where all sacred fords arrive and deities reside by the millions.
Whoever, having reached Prabhāsa sacred field, seeks another sacred ford, / casts away what is in his hand and licks his elbow instead.
The ancestors recited this ancient verse, O beloved: / 'If a son is somehow unable to go to Gayā,
then he should go with effort to the supreme sacred ford Goṣpada.
With tubers, roots, or fruits, or with oil-cake and water— / may there be born in our lineage one who offers a śrāddha here!'
Having bathed there with effort, and having invited brahmins most learned in the Vedas / and fed them diligently according to rule in the śrāddha,
an offering of rice balls must be made by those wishing for the satisfaction of their ancestors.

8.9.m:
No lunar day, no lunar mansion, no conjunction or month and so forth [is restricted]; / one should always go there with a mind full of faith.
There is no restriction of time there, since seeing it is the authoritative means. / Going there on Akṣayatṛtīyā is hard to attain, O beloved,
or on the full-moon day of Kārttika, or the seventh day of Māgha, or during the Padmaka festival.
Gifts of gold, gifts of cows, cloth, silver, clarified butter, and sesame seeds / should be given there by a self-controlled man desiring the satisfaction of his ancestors.
Thus has this secret of the sacred ford of great consequence been told to you, O goddess. / It should not be told to wicked-minded, sinful, or cruel-hearted people.
It should be imparted to one endowed with faith and devoted to ancestral rites. / One who knows the Purāṇas should recite it with devotion, especially at the time of a śrāddha.
Thereby satisfaction lasting twelve years arises for the ancestors. / It should be heard constantly by self-restrained men who fear hell,
and it should always be recited with devotion before brahmins while they eat.
Even if a purified man offers water mixed with sesame seeds to his ancestors here,

In Kṛta he is named Janārdana; in Tretā, Madhusūdana; / in Dvāpara, Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and in Kali he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Thus when the four ages arrive again and again, O tamer of enemies, / having established the order of dharma, he returns to that place.
Whoever, fasting on an Ekādaśī, sees that deity, / surely sees the imperishable eternal abode of Hari in that place.
Yellow garments should be given by him to an eminent twice-born. / Bathing and śrāddha should be performed by those desiring the full fruit of pilgrimage.
Thus has the great power of Hari's appointed abode been told to you. / A wise person who hears it with restrained mind or recites it attains the good path.

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to the one situated on the bank of the Devikā, / famous as Jāleśvara, worshipped by gods and asuras.
In the Cākṣuṣa manvantara, when the Dvāpara age arrived, / the liṅga by the name of Jāleśvara was situated on the bank of the Devikā.
It is worshipped by Nāga maidens; mortal men do not see it. / It is full of jewels of great splendour, radiant like the disc of the moon.
From the remembrance of that god, the murder of a brahmin is destroyed.
The goddess said:
How did it come to be named Jāleśvara? At what time did that happen?
What virtues are proclaimed from living together with the virtuous? / What worlds, what merits [are attained]? Tell me all that, O Lord.

8.9.m:
In this very regard, they cite this ancient legend, / the conversation between Nābhāga and Āpastamba, a treasure of austerity.
Formerly, the great seer Āpastamba, self-controlled, foremost of the twice-born, / continually undertook fasting, and the venerable one became steadfast.
Always casting away anger, greed, delusion, and malice, / he entered the pool of water in the midst of the river Devikā,
having fully understood it, O beloved of Śiva, in the delightful sacred field of Prabhāsa. / A long time then passed as he lived there,
standing like an immovable pillar through supreme meditative union. / Then once, fishermen, arriving at that region,
Casting a huge net, they all hauled it in by force. / Then those hunters, proud of their strength, along with that great fish,
lifted the son of Brahmā out of that water. / Seeing him blazing with tapas, the fishermen, overwhelmed with fear,
bowed low with their heads and spoke these words aloud: // 12

The person who wishes entirely to experience the suffering [of others]— / him indeed those seeking liberation call worse than sinful [for suffering's sake?]. // 17

Whatever good deeds are mine, let that go to them; / and whatever evil was done by them, let all of that come to me! // 19 // / Seeing the blind, the wretched, the maimed, the helpless, and the diseased, / he in whom compassion does not arise is a demon: such is my view. // 20 // / He who, though capable, does not protect living beings / fallen into peril of life and overwhelmed by fear, incurs that very sin. // 21
They say that whatever happiness arises for distressed people, / heaven or liberation is not worth a sixteenth part of it. // 22
Therefore, abandoning these miserable, intensely suffering fish, / I will not take even a step, let alone go to the abode of the gods!" // 23
Īśvara said:
Hearing this speech of the ṛṣi, those fishermen became agitated; / and they reported everything that had happened to Nābhāga. // 24
Then Nābhāga too, hearing of it, went there in haste / accompanied by his ministers and royal chaplain to see that son of Brahmā. // 25

8.9.m:
Having duly honored that godlike sage, the king / said: "O venerable one, speak! What shall I do at your command?" // 26

Hearing that statement, the king, together with his ministers and royal chaplain, / filled with great joy, spoke this word to the muni: // 39
"Arise, arise, venerable one! You are indeed purchased, no doubt. / This is the most suitable price for you, O best of munis!" // 40

Since the fire-sanctuaries of brahmins and the shrines of the deities / are purified by cow-dung, what entity could be greater than that? // 43
Cow-urine, cow-dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter— / the five purifiers from cows purify the entire world. // 44

8.9.m:
A person who, self-restrained and pure, recites this mantra at the three junctures of the day, / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of heaven. // 46
Cows must daily be provided with fodder of grass with devotion. / Taking food oneself without having done so, a person incurs a miserable state. // 47
By him fires are properly offered into, ancestors are gratified, / and deities are worshipped—by him who gives the daily offering to cows. // 48
The mantra:
"O daughter of Surabhi, worshipped by the world, goddess situated in the realm of Viṣṇu! / Well-pleased, accept all that is given by me!" // 49
From protecting their young calves, and likewise from scratching cows, / and from protecting those who are emaciated and distressed, a person is exalted in heaven. // 50
Cows are declared to be the beginning, the middle, and the end for a mortal; / and they always protect the nectar of milk and clarified butter for the gods. // 51
Therefore, cows should be gifted and perpetually honored. / For they are constructed as a stairway, as it were, leading to heaven. (52)

8.9.m:
Having heard this supreme māhātmya of cows, those Niṣādas, / bowing down to the high-souled Āpastamba, then spoke: (53)
The Niṣādas said:
Conversation, darśana, touch, recitation of name, and remembrance— / these indeed are purifying regarding good men; so it is heard. (54)
Conversation and darśana have indeed been made by you with us. / Therefore, bestow your favor; let this cow be accepted! (55)
Āpastamba said:
I accept this cow from you. Freed from sin, / go to heaven, O Niṣādas, along with the fish drawn from the water! (56)
If by producing pleasure for living beings, even through a censured act, / I see hell, then that will dwell as heaven itself. (57)
Whatever good deed may have been done by me through acts of mind, speech, and body, / by that let all who are afflicted by suffering attain a blessed state! (58)

Then, by the grace of that great seer of cultured soul, / by that utterance those Niṣādas went to heaven along with the fish. (59)

Seeing those who lived on fish departing for heaven along with the fish, / the king, accompanied by ministers and servants, said this in astonishment: (60)
Virtuous men are to be served by seekers of welfare, like waters at a sacred ford; / even a moment's attendance upon whom does not become fruitless. (61)
One should always sit with the virtuous; one should hold wholesome conversation with the virtuous; / one should conduct oneself according to the observance of the virtuous; one should practice nothing with the non-virtuous. (62)
Through association with the virtuous, these men who lived on fish / have reached heaven together with the fish, like men who perform meritorious deeds. (63)
There the sage Āpastamba and the great-minded Lomaśa / gratified that king with various desired boons. (64)
Then he chose a disposition toward righteousness, which is very difficult to obtain. / Saying “So be it,” the two of them praised that king with affection: (65)
Ah, you are blessed, O king of kings, since your mind is intent on righteousness! / Righteousness is very difficult to attain for men, particularly for rulers of the earth. (66)

If a king seized with pride does not abandon his own duty, / then who in the world could be superior to him as a man? (67)
Certain is rebirth always for kings, and delusion is also always certain; / and from delusion, hell is certain. Therefore the wise revile kingship. (68)
Men greedy for sensory objects hold kingship in high esteem; / but the wise see that very thing as equal to hell. (69)
..
Therefore, pride, which ruins both worlds, must not be cultivated by you, / if, O great king, you desire an eternal destination for yourself. (70)
Īśvara said:
Having spoken thus, those two high-souled ones went to their respective hermitages. / Nābhāga too, having obtained the boon, entered the city overjoyed. (71)
This glory originating from the Devikā has been declared to you, O goddess. / And at that time Bhava was established as Jāleśvara by the seer. (72)
Since that best of seers fell into the net of the fishermen, / he is renowned on the earth's surface by the name Jāleśvara. (73)

Having bathed there, O great goddess, through the worship of Jāleśvara, / Āpastamba, Nābhāga, and the Niṣādas who lived on fish (74)
went to heaven together with the fish, by virtue of the Devikā. / On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, (75)
he who offers a piṇḍa to the ancestors—his [merit] has no end. / A gift of a cow is to be given there to a brahmin who has mastered the Vedas; (76a-b)
and the māhātmya must be heard, and Jālakeśvara must be beheld. (76c-d)
Thus ends the three hundred thirty-eighth chapter, named 'Description of the Glory of Jāleśvara' in the Māhātmya of the Devikā River, in the first Māhātmya of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, in the seventh Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
Next, O great goddess, one should go to the well celebrated in the three worlds / on the charming bank of the Devikā, which fills up simply by the sound ‘huṃ’. (1)
Then its water goes downward again, O lovely lady. / In ancient times, a [sage] named Taṇḍin was stationed on the bank of the Devikā. (2)

8.9.m:
He performed austerity, O great goddess, dedicated to devotion to Śiva. / As he was thus practicing austerity in that region, O fair-faced one, (3)
an old, blind-eyed deer came to that region, O beloved. / It fell into a deep, great pit devoid of water. (4)
..
Seeing it, that sage, filled with compassion and maintaining silence, / uttered the sound ‘huṃ’ there again and again, O lovely lady. (5)
Then, by the sound ‘huṃ’ made by him, the pit was filled up. / Then the deer emerged with difficulty from the water, O beloved. (6)
Assuming a human form, it questioned that seer, / having experienced extreme wonder, regarding the fruit of action that grants desires: (7)
“I had fallen here in the state of a deer, and have come out having become a man.” / That best of the twice-born explained to him the greatness of that water: (8)
“Hence I have attained human status; there is no other reason here.” / Then that water entered the earth again. (9)
Then that seer, filled with curiosity, uttered ‘huṃ’ again; / once again the well was filled with water as before. (10)

Then he performed his ritual ablution and libation to the ancestors, / recognizing the supreme sacred ford there; thereupon he reached the highest state. (11)
Even today, when ‘huṃ’ is uttered there, a flood of water flows forth. / A man who goes there with devotion, even if intent on sin, (12)
does not obtain rebirth as a human on the earth's surface. / Having bathed there and become pure, the man who performs a śrāddha (13)

There, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, O fair lady, whoever devotes himself to fasting and keeps a vigil,
goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells. / 2
Thus ends the three hundred and fortieth chapter, entitled "The Description of the Greatness of Caṇḍīśvara," in the Devikāmāhātmya, in the first [part], the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, in the seventh [section], the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
Then one should go to the stainless Āśāpūra Vighnarāja, who removes obstacles, situated to the north-west of Śaśibhūṣaṇa.
Because he fulfills desires (āśā), he is remembered as Āśāpūraka. / 1
Where, O queen of gods, having worshipped Vighneśa, Rāma along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa obtained their cherished desire; / 2
Where, O goddess, having worshipped the lord of the gaṇas, the Moon previously obtained his cherished desire: the destruction of all leprosy. / 3

Not far to its south-southwest is situated a sin-removing liṅga installed by the Moon himself, O goddess. / 1

shall obtain the fruit of a thousand years of austerity. Right there, O goddess, is a pond constructed by the Moon, / 3

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the supreme Kapileśvara, to the east of Śīrābhūṣaṇa and west of Koṭitīrtha, / 1
to the south of Jaradgaveśa, and north of the ocean. Indeed, this sacred field of Kapila is not attained by unmeritorious men. / 2
Where in ancient times, O goddess, Kapila performed severe austerity for more than ten thousand years, having installed Maheśvara. / 3
There the divine, great river Kapiladhārā was invoked. Even today, it is seen in the midst of the ocean by the meritorious. / 4

8.9.m:
Having bathed there, O great goddess, especially on Kapilāṣaṣṭhī, one should donate a tawny cow (kapilā) there; he obtains the fruit of [donating] ten million cows. / 5
This is remembered as the expiation for all sins. Having worshipped Kapileśvara, one obtains the fruit of [giving away] ten million maidens. / 6
The Goddess said:
It is a wonder to me, O lord of gods, O Maheśvara! I wish to hear the procedure for Kapilāṣaṣṭhī, beginning with the donation mantras. / 7
Īśvara said:
If in the course of a lifetime even one such ṣaṣṭhī endowed with these conjunctions is attained by men, what more can I say, O goddess? / 8
If Tuesday falls on the sixth day (ṣaṣṭhī) of the dark fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, along with Vyatīpāta and the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra], that is remembered as Kapilā [Ṣaṣṭhī]. / 9
A man having bathed in that sacred field, or at the auspicious Arkasthala, with earth and white sesamum at the auspicious confluence of the Kapilā, / 10
having completed his bath and recitation, should then offer an arghya to Sūrya with water containing red sandalwood and oleander flowers.

The mango grove named Agastyāmravana is situated in that place, / east of Cintāmaṇi, three hundred bow-lengths to the northeast.
There previously austerity was performed by the great-souled Agastya. 2
The Goddess said:
At what time, O Mahādeva? Tell all in detail! 3
Īśvara said:
Formerly, O woman of excellent complexion, there were terrifying demon hordes / known as the Kālakeyas, who caused the destruction of the three worlds. 4
Then they were all slain by powerful Viṣṇu, / residing in Prabhāsa-kṣetra under the name Slayer of Demons, 5
having assumed the form of a tigress called Cakramukhī. / They were slain by that form; thus he became the Slayer of Demons. 6
The remnants of the slain entered into the ocean, overwhelmed by fear. / Then they deliberated: ‘How can the gods be distressed? 7

Having said 'So be it,' all the gods with Indra, / with minds utterly rejoiced, then went to their own abode. // 50
Therefore, with every effort, when autumn arrives, a human being / should go to the hermitage of Agastya and worship Hāṭakeśa, // 51

Then from there one should go, O great goddess, to Kauraveśvarī; / she was worshipped of old by him after whose name Kurukṣetra [is known]. // 1

Īśvara said:
Then one should go, O great goddess, to Suparṇelā Bhairavī, / five hundred bows' distance to the south of Durgakūṭa. // 1
Of old, O goddess, nectar was brought from Pātāla by Suparṇa; / having seized it, it was set down there while the serpents were watching. // 2
Then, seeing it, the goddess protected it beside the serpents; / therefore she became famed on the surface of the earth as Suparṇelā. // 3
The earth is called ‘ilā’; [and here] she was established by Suparṇa. / Therefore, known by the name Suparṇelā, she destroys sins. // 4
Having bathed right there in the Suparṇakuṇḍa, a man should worship her; / he should give food to brahmins, and that man does not die from calamities. // 5ab
A woman will have living children and be adorned with sons. // 5cd

leaving the city of Dvāravatī, Hari resides right here. / I perform his funeral rites, O goddess, in every yuga. // 7
Going there myself on the conjunction of the twelfth lunar day in Nabhasya, O beloved, / I perform them according to rule, together with eminent brahmins. // 8

Now I shall tell you of his ancient history, O beloved. / Having destroyed all the Yādavas, the mighty Vāsudeva, // 12

went to the shore of the ocean and entered deep meditation, / restraining all his senses and fixing the self in the Self. // 14
In the meantime, there arrived one named Jarā, bow in hand, / the son of a fisherman, very dark-bodied, a killer of fish and a doer of evil. // 15

a person resplendent as a dark blue cloud, with eyes resembling lotuses. / Terrified with fear upon seeing him, trembling, with folded hands,

And whatever other best of men come here and see me, / they shall go to the supreme realm where I eternally abide. / 21
Since I was pierced by you with an arrow on the sole of my auspicious foot, / this place will indeed be known as Bhallatīrtha. / 22
Formerly, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, it was declared to be Harikṣetra." / 23
Īśvara said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished, and the hunter also went to heaven. / Those who perform their ritual ablution here endowed with supreme devotion,
shall gladly go to the realm of Viṣṇu by my grace. / 24
Those devoted to the ancestors who perform a śrāddha here— / their ancestors, being propitiated, shall indeed attain satisfaction. / 25
Therefore, having reached that supreme sacred field with every effort, / the four-armed god must be seen after bathing in the Bhalla sacred ford. / 26
Those who, haughty with the strength of their devotion to me, do not bow to my beloved / Vāsudeva, should not be known as my devotees; they are indeed sinners. / 27

Even if one is my devotee, if he eats on the Ekādaśī day, / my liṅga should not be worshipped by that evil-minded person. / 28
That lunar day which is dear to Viṣṇu is also dear to me; / he who does not fast on it is more sinful than the most sinful. / 29
Likewise, on the occasion of Dvādaśī, near Bhallatīrtha, / whoever worships me with devotion, whether a woman or a man,
195b
for thousands of births there is no destruction of his household. / 7.1.352.30
Thus has been narrated to you, O goddess, the sin-destroying māhātmya / of Bhallatīrtha, which belongs to Viṣṇu and destroys all sins. / 31
There, in the presence of Viṣṇu, to the northwest, is an excellent jar, / and [there is] the famous Bhallatīrtha, where Hari was struck by an arrow. / 32
Garments, footwear, and cows are to be given there in accordance with the rules / to the foremost of brahmins by those desiring the full fruit of pilgrimage. / 33

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-second chapter, named 'The Description of the Māhātmya of Bhallatīrtha', in the first section, the Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, of the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skandapurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. / 352
Īśvara said:
"Then, O great goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Kardamāla, / a sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, which destroys all sins. / 1
When that terrifying single ocean existed, when all moving and unmoving things were destroyed, / when the moon, sun, and fire had perished, and all luminaries had gone to dissolution, / 2
the god Janārdana, having seen the earth submerged in the netherworld, / assumed the form of a boar, O fair-faced lady, and with the tip of his tusk
raised the earth with his head and installed it in its proper place. / 3
Having lifted it up, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these words: / 4
'Stationed in this very place, O goddess, you were rescued by me; / my residence shall always be fixed right here. / 5

8.9.m:
Those who propitiate the ancestors at Kardamāla, O fair-faced lady, / by them they will be propitiated until the end of the kalpa, without a doubt. / 6
When they perform a śrāddha there with vegetables, roots, or fruits, / a śrāddha will have been performed at all sacred fords, O auspicious one! / 7
A person who, having bathed in this sacred ford, beholds me— / even the men, insects, and moths who meet their death [here]—
when dead, they go to heaven by virtue of merit, just like twice-borns. / 8
Then they are born in the continents, wealthy and in an excellent family. / The water that flowed from your body through the piercing of the tusk— / 9
having bathed there, O goddess, a person is not born in the animal womb.' / 7.1.353.10
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O goddess, to the wonder that took place there in ancient times: / a herd of deer, utterly terrified, being pursued by hunters,
entered Kardamāla and instantly attained human form. / 11

8.9.m:
He whose feet are the Vedas, whose tusks are the sacrificial posts, whose teeth are the sacrifices, whose mouth is the offering-ladles, / whose tongue is the sacred fire, whose body-hair is the darbha grass, whose head is the Veda, endowed with great austerity, / 7.1.353.20

..

having the Upākarma rite as lips, the Pravargya rite as curl and ornament, / the course of various Vedic meters as his gait, and strides conforming to the sequence proclaimed by Brahmā,
having become this Sacrifice-Boar, he then lifted up the earth. / As he lifted the earth, the tip of his tusk emerged outside.
In that sacred field of Prabhāsa, it was smeared with mud (kardama); / because of that tusk-tip, O goddess, it is remembered as Kardamāla.
There is the great reservoir Daṇḍodbheda where the tusk was firmly placed; / water drawn up by that tusk is like an ablution in a crore of Gaṅgās.

8.9.m:
There extends an eternal sacred field of Viṣṇu measuring just one gavyūti. / And those who have gone to another land, if they die at Daṇḍodbheda,
go to the world of Viṣṇu for thousands of kalpas.
Whoever beholds the Boar at Kardamāla, O great goddess, / even if associated with a crore of acts of violence, he shall attain the highest state.
Sin committed across ten lifetimes is destroyed by darśana of him, O beloved; / the accumulation of sin that was committed in thousands of other lives,
having seen the Boar at Kardamāla, it will go to destruction. / Giving thousands of crores of gold pieces and hundreds of crores of cows—
the merit one obtains [from that] is obtained by a single darśana of the Boar. / In the Kali yuga, exceedingly terrible and bringing fear to living beings,
liberation does not arise elsewhere, except at the Boar's sacred field.
This essential teaching has been proclaimed in brief to you, O goddess: / the māhātmya of Kardamāla, which destroys all sins.

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to Devagupteśvara, O beloved, / there in the north-west, where Soma performed austerity.
Having hidden himself because of leprosy, he stood with downcast face out of shame, / for a thousand divine years, in the excellent sacred field of Prabhāsa.
Then Śiva, the lord of all the gods, became visible; / he was pleased with the Moon and brought about the destruction of his wasting disease.
Then, freed from the wasting disease, the hare-marked [Moon], / having established a great liṅga worshipped by gods and asuras,
since he performed austerity hidden (gupta), it is therefore remembered as Gupteśvara. / That god removes all leprosy through darśana and even through touch.

Īśvara said: / Then, O great goddess, one should go to the god Bahusuvarṇaka, / in the eastern region of Hiraṇyā, at the site called Bahusuvarṇaka,

Thus, in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, in the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses], in the seventh Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the first Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the three hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, entitled 'Description of the Bahusuvarṇeśvaramāhātmya.'
Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the unsurpassed Śṛṅgeśvara / in the presence of Śukasthāna, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed right there according to rule, a man should worship Śṛṅgeśa; / he would be freed from all sins, just as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was of old.
Thus, in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, in the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses], in the seventh Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the first Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the three hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, entitled 'Description of the Śṛṅgeśvaramāhātmya.'

In the north-eastern direction from that is known Koṭinagara; / in its southern region, situated just a yojana away,
is the great liṅga Koṭīśvara, granting the fruit of a crore of sacrifices.
Having bathed there according to the injunction, whoever worships that liṅga / is freed from all sins and obtains the fruit of a crore of sacrifices.
Thus, in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, in the collection of eighty-one thousand [verses], in the seventh Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, in the first Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, entitled 'Description of the Koṭīśvaramāhātmya.'
Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the sacred ford named Nārāyaṇa; / in the north-eastern direction from it is the stepwell proclaimed as Śāṇḍilya.
Having bathed right there according to rule, whoever worships Śāṇḍilya, / or a devoted wife [who does so] according to rule on Ṛṣipañcamī,
touching or not touching, she will surely be freed from fear of the impurity of menstruation.

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the place named Śṛṅgasaras.
And there is installed a god named Śṛṅgāreśvara, / where Hari, accompanied by the gopīs, properly made adornment (śṛṅgāra).
And by that he is named Śṛṅgāreśvara, destroying masses of sins; / whoever worships Bhava residing in that place according to rule—
he will nowhere in the world be touched by poverty or sorrow. (3)

Then, O great goddess, one should go to the [place] situated on the bank of the Hiraṇyā / named Ghaṭikāsthāna, where formerly a seer attained perfection (1)
within a single nāḍī, namely Mṛkaṇḍu, through the yoga of meditation, O lovely-faced one. / Right there a liṅga was installed under the name Mārkaṇḍeśvara, (2ab)
which pacifies all sins through its darśana and through worship. (2cd)
Thus ends the three hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled 'Description of the Glory of Mārkaṇḍeśvara,' in the first [sub-section], 'The Glory of Prabhāsa Field,' of the seventh section, Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. (360)
Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to [the place called] Maṇḍūkeśvara. / Indeed, a liṅga named Māṇḍūkyāyana is installed there. (1)
There, O goddess, is the pool Koṭihrada, and likewise Koṭīśvara Śiva; / there also resides the host of the Mothers, granting the fruits of desires. (2)
Having bathed in the sacred ford of Koṭihrada, whoever worships that liṅga / and worships the Mothers right there is freed from pain and grief. (3)

One yojana to the east of it, O queen of gods, is the pure [spot] / famed as Tritakūpa, destroying all sins, (4ab)
because all sacred fords reside right there, O goddess. (4cd)

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go north of Goṣpada / two gavyūtis away, to the well-known [place] called Valāya. (1)
There, O beloved, are the regional liṅgas of the eleven Rudras, / bearing names such as Ajaikapād and Ahirbudhnya. (2ab)
Whoever worships them according to the rules is freed from all sins. (2cd)

Īśvara said:
Then, O great goddess, one should go to the place situated on the bank of the Hiraṇyā / named Tuṇḍapura, where that pool Gharghara is located. (1)
There is the god Kandeśvara, where my matted hair was tied up. / Having properly bathed there, a man who worships that god, (2ab)
freed from terrible sins, shall attain an auspicious realm. (2cd)

On the Sarasvatī, on the other hand, there is no number to the liṅgas. / Thus adorned with a garland of liṅgas, the five-faced [stream], O goddess— (5)
the Sarasvatī of five streams, O goddess, is spoken of in Prabhāsa, / by whose currents the sacred field of twelve yojanas is intersected. (6)
The water born anywhere there in reservoirs and wells / is to be known as belonging to Sarasvatī; fortunate are those who drink it. (7)
Wherever a person bathes, endowed with proper faith, / he obtains the fruit of a ritual ablution in the Sarasvatī; of this there is no doubt. (8)
The touch-liṅga that is declared, celebrated as glorious Someśa— / the liṅgas of Prabhāsa field are portions of that very Śaṅkara. (9)
Worshipping any liṅga situated in the center of the sacred field, / knowing it to be glorious Someśa, Someśa becomes worshipped. (10)
